articles.title: Tibet earthquake kills at least 16
articles.summary: A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening, killing at least 16 people, injuring 46 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media…

image.caption: The U.S. Geological Survey said a magnitude 7 earthquake rocked northern Tibet on Thursday. (U.S. Geological Survey)

blocks.text: World·New

A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening, killing at least 16 people, injuring 46 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Chinese state media reports communication in part of the region has been down

Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. Among the injured, 11 people were in serious condition and the other 35 sustained minor injuries, the media office said.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.

China's official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in part of the region has been down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said.
It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time, with its epicentre 191 kilometres east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake's depth at 18 kilometres.
Nagqu is more than 300 kilometres north of Tibet's capital, Lhasa.

articles.title: Massive student-led rally marches in Belgrade ahead of Serbian election
articles.summary: Student List movement hopes to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in a pivotal vote on Sunday

blocks.text: About 150,000 supporters of Serbia’s opposition student movement rallied in central Belgrade on Thursday, seeking to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in crunch parliamentary elections this weekend.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, wants to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic’s rightwing populist Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in Sunday’s vote.
Civil society groups have said the campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests and misuse of public resources.

“I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country,” Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, said as she arrived for the students’ rally.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible.”

blocks.caption: Crowds streamed into Belgrade’s central Slavija Square from all directions, also filling several blocks of streets around the area. Photograph: Armin Durgut/AP

blocks.text: Sunday’s vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milošević in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.

Waving “Students are winning” flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students and their supporters marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
The Archive of Public Gatherings, an independent crowd-size monitoring group, estimated about 150,000 people gathered at the rally.

“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic – one of 250 candidates on the Student List – told the crowd, which chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, Vucic announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it,” said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vucic delivers a speech at a Serbian Progressive party campaign rally. Photograph: Pierre Crom/Getty Images

blocks.text: Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking.
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
“I’ve been following this fight since the very beginning,” 35-year-old student rally attender Igor said.
“Today is the last rally, and it’s important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations.”

articles.title: Typhoon Rosal still bringing moderate to heavy rain to Batanes
articles.summary: Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, at 4 am on Friday, October 23

blocks.text: ROSAL. Satellite image of Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 23, 2026, 4 am.
JMA
Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, at 4 am on Friday, October 23

items: Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is still affecting Batanes and other parts of Northern Luzon on Friday, October 23.
Rosal is projected to exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Saturday, October 24.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Typhoon Rosal (Champi) continued to affect Batanes and other parts of Northern Luzon on Friday, October 23, even though it has spared the Philippines from landfall.
Rosal was last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 4 am on Friday. The typhoon is moving northwest at only 15 kilometers per hour (km/h).
Its maximum sustained winds had weakened to 155 km/h on Thursday evening, October 22, while its gustiness eased to 190 km/h.
At its peak, Rosal was a super typhoon with maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in a bulletin issued at 5 am on Friday that Rosal is still bringing moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) to Batanes in the coming hours.

Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan, and Isabela may also continue to experience rain with gusty winds due to Rosal on Friday, while the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora are likely to see scattered rain and thunderstorms caused by the typhoon.

PAGASA added that Rosal’s trough or extension is affecting Masbate, Palawan, the Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Basilan, and Tawi-Tawi. These areas could have scattered rain and thunderstorms as well.

articles.title: [Market Rider] SEC’s market maker push and how it can boost PH stock trading
articles.summary: SEC Chairman Francis Lim spearheads a daring undertaking into the realm of market making, in a bid to boost stock market trading in the Philippines

blocks.text: A quote from the legendary Gus Levy of Goldman Sachs perfectly captures what could be the operational and psychological framework of a market maker.

During his time as senior partner, Levy revolutionized Wall Street trading by turning Goldman Sachs into a primary market maker, for in the ’60s and earlier when an institutional investor wanted to sell a massive block of stock when normal daily volume was comparatively too small, the stock price would tank. Levy turned Goldman Sachs into a primary market maker that would use its own cash to buy those massive blocks instantly, taking the risk into its own balance sheet.

As the story goes, a junior trader at Goldman Sachs bought a massive block of stock from a client. Feeling sure he’ll make a profit, he decided to hold on to the position. Gus Levy noticed the giant unhedged position sitting on the books. He looked down at the young trader and said a line that would become the absolute mantra for market makers in the industry: “Young man, you misunderstand our job. We are in the moving business, not the storage business!”

Among those very happy to welcome this daring undertaking into the realm of market making in the Philippine capital market, spearheaded by no less than the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Francis Ed. Lim, are three of the country’s highly respected financial and stock market personalities. They are: Presidential Legislative Liaison Office (PLLO) Secretary Jose Ma. Clemente “Joey” Salceda, Edward “Edward” K. Lee, and Paulino “Paul” S. Soo.

blocks.caption: A deep dive on capital market reforms with SEC Chairman Francis Lim

blocks.text: Salceda has an extensive background in the Philippine financial and stock markets as a top-tier equity analyst and research director prior to entering politics. Lee is the founder and chairman of the country’s largest online stock brokerage firm, COL Financial, while Soo is the chairman and CEO of First Abacus Financial Holdings Corp. and also serves as chairman and president of Abacus Securities Corporation along with its online trading platform, MyTrade PH.
“We have many fundamentally sound Philippine companies trading at attractive valuations. What we lack is liquidity. Now is the time to unlock their value,” Salceda said.

Likewise, Lee is confident that our capital market is vibrant enough for the plan of the SEC to succeed considering developments in the country’s structural architecture on ease of doing business and liberal regulation that is now generally attractive for risk takers.
Truly a longtime proponent for the development of the stock market, he gave these passionate words: “It’s been 30 years. Francis is our only hope.”

A bit more cautious but certainly in about the plan, Soo suggested a careful consideration. He said, “I would be interested to see how the pros and cons are.” He also wondered if there are enough people knowledgeable on how the plan will work.

A seasoned participant of the market, Soo admitted that he has only basic knowledge, not to mention the fact that that has been ages ago, with this deeply truthful message, “I spent one month in New York in the T-Bills market; too long ago.”
The official source for the rules on market making is SEC Memorandum Circular No. 28, Series of 2026, issued on October 15, 2026.
Its stated main purpose is “to establish a formal regulatory framework for market making to improve secondary market liquidity, enhance price discovery, and support capital formation.”
For trading participants applying to act as market makers, capital requirement is set to as low as P150 million minimum unimpaired paid-up capital.

Applicants must also show adequate operational capacity, a satisfactory track record, and designate at least one specialist with a minimum of three years of relevant experience in securities trading or market making.

Financial instruments covered in the rule applies only to equity and fixed-income securities either listed, traded, or enrolled on an exchange under the jurisdiction of the SEC. It does not cover government securities governed by the Bureau of the Treasury’s Primary Dealer framework unless extended.
Incentives are to be extended to participating firms which includes “reduced transaction fees, liquidity rebates, and access to enhanced trading facilities.”

Market makers are to provide continuous quoting services for buy and sell prices of select securities, the submission of quarterly performance reports, and compliance with the provisions for incentive and/or rebate.
Existing market makers have six months to comply and the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) must submit implementation guidelines within 30 days.

Also glad about the new development but has some questions about the plan is the president and chief trader of Eagle Equities Inc., Joseph “Joey” Roxas. His main concern is how the market maker will exactly make a profit considering the various costs involved.
Roxas is referring to the prescribed rules in the market maker’s quoting obligations, spread thresholds, minimum quote sizes, and other related matters in the trading of the related securities.

Supposedly, the entire business model of market making is to keep assets moving like buying at the “bid side,” and immediately selling at the “ask side,” and capturing the tiny difference — the spread — as many times a day as possible. To Roxas, this is not always possible all the time.

For this, “incentives will be a big factor,” Roxas said. In this regard, he would like to know “if it is the stock exchange that would be partially subsidizing liquidity, through what is mentioned as “liquidity rebates.”
As far as he could see, the rebate that may come from the stock exchange could be “the PSE fees based on turnover, which he said is only equivalent to just 0.00001 of the cost of total transaction.

“I hope the implementation guidelines are not so complicated as to turn off prospective market makers, just like what happened in the Securities Borrowing and Lending (SBL) policy of the short selling program of the PSE,” Roxas added.

Another market veteran is H.E. Bennett Securities Inc.’s market strategist and chief trader, Joel de la Peña. He finds the P150 million capital requirement may be too small for a market maker. In the market heydays of the past, he said “I know about a group of traders has a budget on hand of P1 billion to day trade.”

De la Peña also suggested that the SEC and PSE control the “manipulative” acts of listed companies that may derail and imperil the financial health of market makers. As to how, De la Peña says, “For one, just look back at the delisting stories in the market.”

On the overall, the plan is without a doubt welcome. This is captured by the enthusiastic proffered comment of Andro Leo “Andoy” I. Beltran, vice president of First Metro Securities Brokerage Corporation (FirstMetroSec): “This is a welcome development for the Philippine stock market and one that we at FirstMetroSec can relate to from firsthand experience. This is a positive step toward developing a deeper, more liquid, and more efficient capital market, especially as the PSE introduces new products.”

“Market making has been allowed in the Philippine stock market since 2013, when the ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) framework was introduced. Since the launch of the then First Metro Philippine Equity Exchange-Traded Fund (FMETF), now ATR FAMI ETF (AETF), FirstMetroSec has served as its market maker. What is new now is the expansion of market making beyond ETFs to other eligible securities and products, including Global Philippine Depositary Receipts (GPDRs).

“Some securities may not naturally attract enough buyers and sellers, especially when they are newly introduced or their markets are still developing. Market makers can help bridge this gap, and effectively give investors greater assurance that they can enter or exit positions freely.

“Of course, market making is not a silver bullet. But this is one that may help build a Philippine stock market where investors can transact more efficiently, companies can access capital more effectively, and more Filipinos can participate in long-term wealth creation.”

Edward Lee offered the wisdom of the following quote as to calm the fears on the adverse effects the plan may present: “If you try to protect your investors too much from bad companies, from failing investments, and from horrible mistakes, it may not lead you to a vibrant market. You have to allow for mistakes. You have to allow people to deal with the consequences. Do not rush in to bail them out from their overreach.”
In short, “it’s education, not protection” should be our attitude toward the proposed plan, Lee added. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com

articles.title: Australia offers astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg for space mission to International Space Station
articles.summary:
Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission

  • Get our
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station.
The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag.

The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund.

Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost.
“We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.”
Bennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024.

She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30.
In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”.

In August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according to The Australian, described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and ­technology”.
South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid.

“South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity.

“Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.”

A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term economic sense for Australia beyond the usual sensibilities of the Treasury bean counters”.
after newsletter promotion

Richard de Grijs, a professor of physics and astronomy at Macquarie University, said of Bennell-Pegg: “She is qualified, she has undergone significant training, so she is set to go up if a suitable mission can be found.

“The government has actually contributed quite a lot of money to that education already,” he said. The ASA paid $466,000 for Bennell-Pegg to complete her astronaut training at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany.
“There is an inspirational value in sending a citizen from your country to space who is also the Australian of the Year … but the question is, is that worth $100m?” De Grijs said.
“It’s a lot of money, but on the other hand, it might actually lead to returns that are way more than the estimated number.”
de Grijs pointed out that Australia was also involved in “inspirational spaceflight” by another means: an Australian-built lunar rover, named Roo-ver, will be sent to moon on a Nasa mission in 2030.
Darin Lovett, chair of the Space Industry Association of Australia, said the industry had “a strong track record of return on investment”.

“For around $100m, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.”
In a speech Bennell-Pegg deliveredearlier this month, she described space as “a gateway – a lure – into the full breadth of STEM fields. Especially for those that dream of going up there.”

articles.title: 'They destroyed my life': 2 Sask. men imprisoned for exploiting woman from Bangladesh
articles.summary: A Bangladeshi woman who was trafficked and exploited by two men in Saskatchewan — and repeatedly raped by one of them — says she now lives in fear and struggles to trust anyone.

image.caption: Sohel Haider, left, and Mohammed Masum pay for parking in front of Saskatoon provincial court on Wednesday, June 3, 2026. They are now both in custody serving sentences for human trafficking. (Hannah Spray/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
A Bangladeshi woman who was trafficked and exploited by two men in Saskatchewan — and repeatedly raped by one of them — says she now lives in fear and struggles to trust anyone.
Mohammed Masum, Sohel Haider sentenced for human trafficking
"I can't forget them. They stopped my dream. They destroyed my life. They ruined my honour, my future, my family, my career," the woman wrote in her victim impact statement.
Mohammed (M.D.) Masum, 45, and Sohel Haider, 56, were convicted earlier this year of human trafficking and returned to Saskatoon provincial court on Thursday for their sentencing.

Masum was also found guilty of three counts of sexual assault, for actions that the judge classified "in clearer and simpler layman's language" as rapes. The victim's identity is protected by a court-ordered publication ban.

Even though her name has not been published, she said in her victim impact statement that the gossip in her home community in Bangladesh has affected her family's honour and ruined her siblings' futures.

The woman said she used to be independent and self-sufficient, but now depends on others for support and struggles with that. She questions her decision to come to Canada, where she felt like a product being sold to a customer.

items: 2 Sask. restaurant operators convicted of trafficking woman from Bangladesh

blocks.text: The charges covered a period between Aug. 1, 2022, and March 31, 2023. The woman came to Saskatchewan after being told she would have a job in a restaurant that would help her stay in the country as a temporary foreign worker.

She worked first at a restaurant Haider operated in Gull Lake, then she was sent to Tisdale to work in a restaurant operated by Masum. They did not have the proper work permits for her, but said they were working on it. She was not properly paid and was forced to work long hours, six days a week.
When she finally received a work permit, it was for a different restaurant in Elrose. Shortly after arriving there, the woman fled with the help of some people who had become concerned about her.
Trust violated, Crown argues
Human trafficking carries a mandatory minimum sentence of four years in prison.

Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning argued that Masum's crimes — one count of human trafficking and three counts of sexual assault — called for a total sentence of 15 years in prison, and Haider should be sentenced to five and a half years for the human trafficking.
Dunning argued both offenders were in positions of trust and authority over the woman, and they violated that trust by controlling "virtually every aspect of her life" after she came to Saskatchewan.
In addition, Masum exploited the woman "for his own sexual gratification" in a series of sexual assaults, including some that involved physical violence, Dunning argued.
Masum's lawyer Zachary Carter argued for a total sentence of seven to nine years, suggesting that is still a "substantial" sentence.

Haider's lawyer Chris Gratton argued for the mandatory minimum of four years, arguing there was an absence of aggravating factors that would push the sentence higher than the minimum, which is itself a significant sentence.
Restitution ordered
Judge Miguel Martinez delivered his sentencing decision late Thursday afternoon.
He agreed with Gratton that Haider should serve the mandatory minimum sentence of four years.
For Masum, the judge imposed a total sentence of 14 years.
He also ordered both men to pay restitution to the victim for wages owed to her. Haider was ordered to pay $5,885.16 and Masum was ordered to pay $12,268.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Rebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10
articles.summary:
NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued

Australian A-lister Rebel Wilson has secured a major…

blocks.text: Australian A-lister Rebel Wilson has secured a major court victory after co-producers of her debut film accused her of sabotage, lying and breaching contracts.
The Pitch Perfect star directed, co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US.
It had a budget of $22m but made just $335,000 at the local box office, which Wilson’s co-producers allege could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.

The Bridesmaids star claimed in posts from July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star.
The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could purchase it from them.
On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden in the New South Wales supreme court awarded the trio $10 in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons.

Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.
The judge awarded her $359,000 plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgment.
It was the second victory for Wilson after she was cleared of defaming her debut film’s star Charlotte MacInnes earlier this year following a fiery federal court hearing.
MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.
The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.
MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.
The federal court found none of Wilson’s posts were defamatory.

articles.title: Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media
articles.summary: A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake has struck Tibet in southwestern China, official media reported. Chinese state TV said it's the strongest quake to hit the remote Himalayan region in five years.

image.caption: Earthquakes are relatively common in China [FILE: Nov 14, 2017]Image: Ivan Damanik/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A strong earthquake struck Tibet in southwestern China on Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring 32 others, Chinese state media reported.
Hundreds of homes in the remote Himalayan region collapsed due to the magnitude 7.0 quake, Xinhua reported.
The earthquake is the strongest to hit the region in the past five years, broadcaster CCTV said, and the most powerful to hit China since January 2024.
How severe was the earthquake in Tibet?
At least 339 residential buildings have collapsed, local government officials said, according to state media. Twenty livestock sheds were also destroyed.
Of the dozens injured, 11 were in a serious condition, the local media office said.
Disaster relief efforts were ongoing as officials assess the scale of the damage, the state news agency added.
Xinhua reported that power and communication lines to the area were also disrupted.
What do we know about the area where the earthquake struck?
The earthquake's epicenter is around 190 kilometers (120 miles) northeast of Nagqu, a city around 300 kilometers north of the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.
The mountainous area is sparsely populated.
The quake struck at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.
How often do earthquakes hit China?
Earthquakes are relatively common in China.
In January 2025, a quake near Mount Everest in Tibet's Tingri region killed at least 126 people.
In 2010, at least 2,698 people were killed when a magnitude 7.1 quake hit Qinghai province, which neighbors Tibet.

articles.title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
articles.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.

blocks.text: "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.

But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.

They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.

Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.

Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.

Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".

Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".

Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.

This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

articles.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
articles.summary: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.

blocks.text: A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.

The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."

That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".

In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.

They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.

In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.

"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.

"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.

Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.

"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.

"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.
Additional reporting by Peter Mwai
Maps and graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry, Jake Friend and Matt Mitchell-Camp

articles.title: A possible three tornados wallop Arizona, bringing golf-ball sized hail
articles.summary:
Violent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and trees and carried thunder and heavy winds through state

Yet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four…

blocks.text: Yet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four Corners region surveyed blown-away roofs, trees knocked onto homes and power lines downed from overnight tornadoes that injured one person.

The injuries weren’t life-threatening but rare for an area better known for scalding heat. But this fall has been unusually soggy in the south-west with El Niño conditions that have sent one tropical system after another in from the Pacific, causing the Grand Canyon and surrounding deserts to rage with floods.

Now, golf ball-size hail and tornadoes have joined the mix. National Weather Service meteorologists suspect at least three tornadoes touched down as storms swept across central Arizona late Wednesday.

The nasty weather hit during Lenna Landy’s yoga routine in Overgaard, a community of about 3,000 people 140 miles (225km) north-east of Phoenix. Landy had ignored alerts about a possible tornado, but then the storm struck.
“It was like Zeus-was-angry kind of level, of thunder cracks,” Landy said.
The power went off, her house shook and Landy couldn’t find her glasses.
“If this is my end, I won’t see it coming,” she recalled thinking. “The scariest part was just like, how quickly it came on.”
The storm peeled off nearby roofs, shattered windows and blew a shed into a home, she said. A spruce tree in her yard was split in half.

blocks.caption: A storm dumps heavy rain and hail across Flagstaff, Arizona, on Wednesday. Photograph: Cheyanne Mumphrey/AP

blocks.text: Still more severe weather, including large hail, struck Thursday with much of Arizona under tornado and flood watches. Similar weather soaked New Mexico, while swathes of Utah and Colorado were under flood watches and warnings.

Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming in from the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.

blocks.caption: Uprooted trees cause damage at an apartment complex after storms hit the area on Wednesday in Mesa, Arizona. Photograph: Ross D Franklin/AP

blocks.text: Tornadoes are somewhat but not exceptionally unusual in Arizona. Notable outbreaks happened in 2019 and 2010.

Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines more than 30ft (9 meters) tall fell down in the Coconino national forest, north-west of Flagstaff.
“These are not small trees that are down,” Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”

articles.title: Part 2: Old-timer bets in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice
articles.summary: These bets are part of the list of candidates who vied for the justice post in 2025 that ultimately went to Associate Justice Raul Villanueva

blocks.text: Last of 2 partsPart 1: New candidates in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will pick his second Supreme Court (SC) associate justice appointee in November.

This is for the position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier, who is set to retire on November 16. The magistrate will be Marcos’ second appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025.
So far, there are 19 applicants in total, majority of whom are incumbent government officials.
The Judicial and Bar Council, tasked to screen the candidates and submit a short list of nominees to Marcos, divided the bets into two categories.
New applicants attended the public interviews on October 13 and 15, while the old bets no longer took part in the event because their past interviews are still valid.
Get to know the old-timer bets vying to replace Associate Justice Lazaro Javier below.

items: Current Court of Appeals (CA) associate justice and chairperson of the 6th Division.
Appointed to the CA on March 11, 2010, and set to retire from the judiciary on December 13, 2033.
She served as presiding judge of Metropolitan Trial Court Branch 30 in 2000, and then was promoted in the same court as its first vice executive judge.
Antonio Valenzuela was appointed in 2005 as Presiding Judge of Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 28. She was later recognized as outstanding RTC judge of Manila.
She previously taught at Saint Scholastica’s College and Adamson University. The CA justice was also part of the SC applicants in 2014, 2020, and 2025.

She was part of the CA division, which upheld the dismissal of the case against journalist Lady Ann Salem and trade unionist Rodrigo Esparago, both of whom were arrested when former president Rodrigo Duterte targeted progressives.
Current CA associate justice and chairperson of the Second Division.

Bato is the second most senior justice in the appellate court, next to Presiding Justice Fernanda Lampas Peralta. He was appointed to the CA on March 15, 2004, and will retire from the judiciary on August 27, 2028.
He obtained his law degree from Silliman University. Before his CA appointment, Bato was a court attorney in the SC and served as a trial court judge in Imus, Cavite, and in Dumaguete City.
While in the SC, he co-founded the Supreme Court Assembly of Lawyer-Employees and was elected as its first vice president and later as president.
Bato wrote the decision that dismissed the double murder case against former national police chief and senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson in the Dacer-Corbito case.
He was also part of the CA division that upheld the cyber libel conviction of Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa and former Rappler researcher Reynaldo Santos Jr. in 2022
The CA justice was also among the SC applicants in 2011, 2017, and 2025.
Current Solicitor General who oversees the Office of the Solicitor General, the government’s primary legal counsel. Appointed by Marcos to the position in May 2025.
Former dean of the University of the Philippines (UP) College of Law.
Prior to her deanship appointment in November 2023, she was the former chief executive officer of the Pag-IBIG fund.
Previously, Berberabe was a senior lecturer at the UP College of Law, and a professorial lecturer on jurisprudence and legal philosophy at the Philippine Judicial Academy.

She obtained her philosophy degree from UP, graduating summa cum laude and class valedictorian of the College of Social Sciences and Philosophy in 1989. She became the first female instructor of philosophy in UP. Berberabe was also the salutatorian of her UP law class in 1999.
Philippine Basketball Association legend Avelino “Samboy” Lim, who passed away in December 2023, was her husband.

In March this year, the OSG filed a position with the SC asking for the acquittal of Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and former researcher Reynaldo Santos Jr. in their Duterte-time cyber libel case.
Under Berberabe too, the SC put an end to the Securities and Exchange Commission’s shutdown order against Rappler. This was because the OSG no longer pursued appealing the case.
CA associate justice and chairperson of the 3rd Division.
A native of Bicol.
He was appointed to the CA on November 05, 2009, and will retire from the judiciary on August 25, 2027.
Cruz concurred in the CA decision that voided a 2018 shutdown order against Rappler by the SEC, and ordered the restoration of the news organization’s certificate of incorporation.
He also concurred in the CA decision that sentenced US Marine Joseph Scott Pemberton to a maximum of 10 years in prison for killing transwoman Jennifer Laude in 2014.
CA associate justice and chairperson of the 9th Division.
Appointed to the CA on February 22, 2012, and will retire from the judiciary on April 25, 2036.
Sempio Diy is the daughter of former CA justice Alicia Sempio-Diy, a known family law expert.
She earned her psychology degree from the Ateneo de Manila University in 1986, and then her law degree from San Beda University later on. She ranked third in her graduating class.
Before her CA appointment, Sempio Diy served as Quezon City RTC judge from 2005 to 2012, and then as Municipal Trial Court judge in Quezon City from 2001 to 2005.
In 2015, it was Sempio-Diy who penned the CA decision that said the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority has no power to implement its anti-smoking campaign.

She is the ponente of the CA ruling that approved the phase out of 15-year-old buses in 2016. She also concurred in the CA ruling that stopped a Manila court order that questioned the Philippine-US extradition treaty.
CA associate justice and chairperson of the 4th Division.
She was appointed to the CA on March 11, 2010, and will retire from the judiciary on June 24, 2033.
She served as examiner for Ethics and Practical Exercises during the 2016 Bar Examinations.
Garcia Fernandez is the ponente of the ruling that affirmed the dismissal of over 200 Coke employees in 2014.

In 2018, Garcia Fernandez wrote the CA ruling that denied the petition filed by a cop who’s a supect in the killing of South Korean businessman Jee Ick-joo. The cop sought to reverse the ruling of the Angeles City, Pampanga Regional Trial Court that granted the motion to discharge one of the co-accused in the case and turn him into a state witness.
She also concurred in the the CA ruling that affirmed the ban on field trials of genetically-modified eggplant in the country.
Current CA presiding justice and chairperson of the First Division.
She was appointed to the CA on February 9, 2004, and will retire from the judiciary on June 16, 2030.
She is the wife of former chief justice Diosdado Peralta. They have four children.
Lampas Peralta earned her law degree from San Beda University in 1984.
She worked in the corporate world as a certified public accountant and lawyer, before working under the Office of the Solicitor General in 1986.
Lampas Peralta is among the justices who concurred in the CA decision that denied the application for protective writs of red-tagged environmental activists Jonila Castro and Jhed Tamano.

In 2013, she also concurred in the CA ruling that affirmed its decision clearing former Palawan governor Joel Reyes in the 2011 killing of broadcaster and environmentalist Gerry Ortega. The SC ordered Reyes’ rearrest in 2023, and the suspect has been under custody since September 2024.

During chief justice Maria Lourdes Sereno’s bout with her quo warranto case, Sereno aimed for the exclusion of then-associate justice Diosdado Peralta and three other justices in her case. Sereno claimed the then-associate justice had bias because he believed it was Sereno who decided to exclude Lampas Peralta from the list of applicants for CA presiding justice in 2017. Sereno claimed Peralta himself said this in at least two impeachment hearings.
Current CA associate justice, chairperson of the 12th Division.
Appointed to the CA on May 13, 2015, and will retire from the judiciary on October 08, 2034.
He had previously applied for the SC associate justice post.

Martin is the ponente of the CA decision that affirmed the Office of the Ombudsman’s ruling to perpetually bar former Makati mayor Jejomar Erwin “Junjun” Binay Jr. from holding office over irregularities in the P1.3-billion Makati Science High School building project.
He is also the ponente of the CA decision that ordered the reinstatement and the award of full back wages and benefits of GMA Network’s 51 workers fired for protesting their non-regularization.
Current Sandiganbayan associate justice, chairperson of the Third Division. Appointed to the anti-graft court on January 20, 2016, and will retire from the judiciary on October 9, 2027.

He earned his business management degree from the Ateneo de Manila University, and his law degree from the UP College of Law. He holds a master’s degree in public administration from the John F. Kennedy School of Government in Harvard University.

He joined the Office of the Solicitor General in 1986, and was appointed Assistant Solicitor General in 1999, heading the Sedfrey A. Ordoñez Division. Under the OSG, he worked on big ticket cases like Sarah Balabagan’s appeal and the Flor Contemplacion case.
He also taught persons deprived of liberty inside the New Bilibid Prison studying to complete their degrees while detained.

At the Sandiganbayan, he was involved in many cases. He concurred in the anti-graft court’s ruling that affirmed the conviction of former Maguindanao governor Datu Sajid Ampatuan on 130 criminal cases. He also voted in favor of affirming Ampatuan’s graft and malversation conviction involving P400 million in public funds meant for farm-to-market roads in Maguindanao.

Miranda concurred in the decision that acquitted Senator JV Ejercito of technical malversation over the alleged unlawful diversion of San Juan City’s calamity fund when Ejercito was the mayor. He also voted in 2020 in favor of the ruling that acquitted Cebu Governor Gwendolyn Garcia in the case involving the province’s purchase of a P98.8-million property that was mostly underwater.
His chamber is currently handling the malversation case of former senator Bong Revilla related to flood control corruption, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta’s plunder charge over his campaign finances.
Miranda is the lone dissenter in the resolution that granted Revilla’s petition for bail. He was outvoted, paving the way for the fomer senator’s temporary freedom.
Current CA Associate Justice, 1st Division senior member.
Appointed to the CA on December 12, 2017, and will retire from the judiciary on October 13, 2038.
Before his appointment in the appellate court, he was shortlisted by the JBC for a Sandiganbayan Associate Justice post. He was also in private practice.
Ong is the brother of former Sandiganbayan associate justice Gregory Ong, who was dismissed in 2014 over his alleged links to pork barrel-implicated Janet Napoles.
He concurred in the CA decision that ordered the reinstatement and the award of full back wages and benefits of GMA Network’s 51 workers fired for protesting their non-regularization.
Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice and chairperson of the 3rd Division.

San Pedro earned her communications degree from UP, finishing cum laude, and receiving the presidential pin and student council service award in 1986. She earned her law degree from the UP College of Law in 1990, graduating in the top 20 of her batch.

She started her career in the judiciary as court attorney in the CA, and then later in the SC. She also served as presiding judge of Pasig City Metropolitan and Regional Trial Courts (RTC), where she handled family and commercial court cases.
In 2011, she was awarded the Judicial Excellence Award (Chief Justice Ramon Avanceña Award) and was one of the three most outstanding judges recognized by the Society for Judicial Excellence.
San Pedro also taught law at the Ateneo de Manila University and served as Mandatory Continuing Legal Education lecturer at the UP Law Center.
She served as Bar examiner twice: for Mercantile Law in 2019, and then for The Law Pertaining to the State and its Relationship with its Citizens in 2020/2021.

As Pasig City judge, she handled Rappler’s securities and code case that stemmed from an anti-dummy complaint. In 2019, she inhibited herself from the case, which was later transferred to a different RTC branch.

articles.title: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit
articles.summary:
Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’

The head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has…

blocks.text: The head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has appealed to King Charles III as a “human brother” whose family he said had benefited from slavery to support reparations talks at next month’s Commonwealth leaders meeting in the Caribbean.

Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next month, professor Hilary Beckles urged the king to use his influence to advance slavery reparations talks between Britain and the Caribbean.

Beckles, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “My personal appeal to King Charles III, not so much in his role as head of the Commonwealth, not so much in his role as the constitutional monarch of the United Kingdom … I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who reflects upon the history of his family, and he can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family.”
He declared that he believed the king was aware that the wealth he is passing on to his children and his grandchildren came from chattel slavery.
Referring to the king as “a man, as a human brother”, he urged Charles to ensure the Commonwealth, historically “the site of this crime”, becomes a “moral institution committed to human justice”.

Beckles’s appeal comes amid growing calls from Caribbean leaders and groups for Charles to formally apologise for slavery when he visits Guyana and the Bahamas next week ahead of Chogm, which he will attend in Antigua.

On Thursday, Commonwealth secretary-general Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey told Sky News that a formal apology for slavery from King Charles “wouldn’t hurt” and that the “time has come” for a serious conversation regarding reparations.
Eric Phillips, head of Guyana’s reparations committee and vice-chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, joined the calls for an apology from the king.

“The king is a decent monarch based on his lifelong commitments to the world in which the environment for him is sacred. We Africans are also part of that sacred environment. As an enlightened monarch, I strongly believe King Charles will want to promote a conversation of decency that reflects his character and values,” he said.
“The citizens of the United Kingdom say, long live the king. We in Guyana say, long live the king, so he can apologize and call for reparations,” he added.

Last month, when Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to King Charles for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March, a palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”.

But David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said he was concerned about a lack of unanimous agreement on commitments on reparations in a draft of the 2026 Chogm communique, which records agreements made by leaders.

Comissiong said a paragraph that referenced the commitment to dialogue made at the previous Commonwealth summit in Samoa and highlights subsequent developments at the UN, African Union and Caricom, was confirmed, but there was disagreement about a second paragraph mandating Commonwealth foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.

“It is very peculiar, to say the least, that the second paragraph which speaks about the Commonwealth foreign affairs ministers coming together to engage in these discussions … has not been unanimously agreed upon,” he said.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations commission, said that campaigners are expected to raise the issue of reparations during the conferences’ major forums, and that discussions between governments are expected to take place at their meetings.

He said the reparations movement will launch a “Global Reparations Caravan”, described as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture, at a separate event on 3 November.

O’Marde added that, while there will be stringent security measures around the event, he expects physical demonstrations from groups who are “inflamed” by the blanket statements of no apology coming out of the UK.
“Blanket no apologies from both government and monarchy reek of gross insensitivity to the demands of the citizens of the Caribbean,” he said.

Beckles stressed that the absence of a dedicated official event at Chogm does not mean that reparations would remain peripheral to the summit. He described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.
“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” he said.

“I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”

articles.title: Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says
articles.summary:
CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care

Thousands of children in England are experiencing some of the sharpest rises…

blocks.text: Thousands of children in England are experiencing some of the sharpest rises in waiting times for healthcare in the history of the NHS, a report has revealed.

While some adult waiting times have improved, children and young people are being “hit hardest” amid soaring demand and falling numbers of staff, according to the annual state of care report by the Care Quality Commission.

In community health services alone, 80,000 children and young people have been waiting more than a year for an appointment – almost 11 times the number of adults, the report said. Experts said that was “wholly unacceptable”. Children’s health conditions were getting worse and becoming harder to treat as a result, they added.

More broadly across health and social care services in England there were signs of improvement, including more GP appointments, increased use of digital solutions and shorter waits for elective care. The report also highlighted examples of local innovation, including neighbourhood models and integrated care teams.
But improvements were struggling to keep pace with rapidly rising demand for health and social care. In many areas, including mental health services, patients’ needs are also becoming more complex.
Persistent inequalities across the entire health and care system mean people’s experience of care is fractured and heavily dependent on where they live and who they are, according to the report.
Across all areas of the country and every part of the health and social care system, there was “unwarranted variation” in access to services, quality of care and outcomes, the CQC said.
Some adults with cancer were waiting far too long to begin treatment after being diagnosed, while there remained “sustained pressure” in urgent and emergency care.

But the report highlighted how children in particular were bearing the brunt of long waiting times. And, despite growing demand, health visitor and school nurse numbers were “continuing to decline”, the CQC said.

It also raised concerns about regional variations in rates of children being admitted to hospital for diabetes and asthma, and sounded the alarm over particularly high rates of rotten teeth among children in some areas.

Dr Ronny Cheung, of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said community health services existed to support some of the country’s most vulnerable children outside hospital, including those with complex conditions, developmental disorders and safeguarding needs.

“Yet these children face some of the longest waits in the NHS, while waiting times for adult community services have improved. It is wholly unacceptable that more than one in four children still wait over a year for treatment, and without urgent action, too many more will be left to suffer unnecessarily.
“As a paediatrician, I am sick of seeing children wait so long for support that they miss crucial opportunities to improve their health and development.”
Behind the figures were children struggling at school, families pushed to breaking point and conditions becoming more complex while they wait, Cheung added.

The CQC chair, Julia Neuberger, said that while some health and social care services were “working well”, improvements were not keeping pace with demand. “To repair a fracturing system, there must be a collective response,” she added.

The Department of Health and Social Care said the report showed “the scale of the challenge this government inherited” when it was elected in 2024. “While the CQC recognises signs of progress on waiting lists, cancer care and general practice, patients and families rightly expect faster improvements – which is why the secretary of state has committed to go further to end corridor care, transform support for mothers and children, and deliver a new national care service,” a spokesperson added.

articles.title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skin care sales
articles.summary: The beauty giant's CEO says the use of GLP-1s is "a very important phenomenon for us".

blocks.text: Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss.
The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".
He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".
L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.

The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.
While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face.

Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.
L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.
Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.
Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.
Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance.
Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs.
