articles.title: New York City council votes to advance bill that would ban horse-drawn carriages
articles.summary: New York City council passed a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring.

image.caption: A horse that takes people on carriage rides through Central Park drinks water at an entrance to the park on Oct. 14. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
New York City council passed a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
Legislation requires mayor to develop plan to transition drivers to new jobs

The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers and the rest of the industry find other jobs, though its provisions are vague and doesn't set clear benchmarks for displaced workers.

Instead, it requires city hall to come up with a program that includes job referrals, career counselling and educational opportunities. It also allows the administration to consider some form of compensation for industry workers.
The mayor's office has been working on a workforce transition program and has started discussions on potential compensation, according to city hall.

"The mayor will sign this bill, and the Mamdani administration is working every day to ensure we can do so while providing the strongest possible protections for the owners and workers in this industry," a spokesperson for the mayor said after the council's vote.
Montreal upholds ban on horse-drawn calèches
The union representing carriage drivers had vowed to file a legal challenge "the minute the ink dries" on the legislation.

The latest push began in June after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after jumping from a runaway carriage during a ride. His death appeared to be the first fatality involving a horse carriage in Central Park since the rides began.

items: Former NHL player happy that horse-drawn vehicles set to be legal in Saskatoon
Teen dies after being thrown from horse-drawn carriage in New York's Central Park

blocks.text: Mahajan's family has personally appealed to the city to end the rides, offering tearful testimony that they thought the rides were safe. His uncle, Gaurav Mahajan, praised the proposal during a rally Thursday, saying "the hour of justice has finally arrived," as he stood beside local lawmakers and animal welfare activists.

"We're turning our shattering loss into an unbreakable shield of kindness for the city. For months, our family hasn't been allowed to just grieve," he said. "We've had to fight. We've had to channel our devastating sorrow into a war for change."
Carriage drivers have expressed sympathy for Mahajan and his family but argue they are being unfairly targeted because of a single accident.

"It does nothing for alternate employment, for the continuation of our businesses," said Christina Hansen, a longtime carriage driver and industry spokesperson. "Who's going to pay my rent while I'm looking for a job?"

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
articles.summary:
• 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’

  • Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record

Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain…

blocks.text: Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s, with the seven-time world champion also stating he believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”
Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.
F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

blocks.caption: Rwanda’s investment in sports sponsorship has led to accusations that it is attempting to sportswash its human rights record. Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

blocks.text: Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.”

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.
after newsletter promotion

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.
Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

articles.title: Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump
articles.summary:
Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing

The latest shudder for stocks in the

blocks.text: The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran .

The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.
Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.
Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.
Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.
after newsletter promotion

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.
But US yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.
The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.

articles.title: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's internet access
articles.summary: Ukraine relies on Starlink for a range of military uses - its owner Elon Musk has repeatedly denied restricting access.

blocks.text: Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's internet access, Donald Trump has said.
The US president was speaking hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk has previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report he had put pressure on Musk to restore access to the service, but when asked about it said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration has previously insisted it did not instruct Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine relies on Starlink - owned by Musk's SpaceX company - for a range of battle communications and early warning systems during Russian missile attacks.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
Speaking at a press conference , he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.

Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

articles.title: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval
articles.summary: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.
The comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.
Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.

“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,” the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian.
He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.
Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.

“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.

“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”

blocks.caption: Miatta Fahnbulleh: ‘It has been really painful to watch the consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change.’ Photograph: Imageplotter/Alamy

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.

The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.

Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”

Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.
“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”

The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”

Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.
“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”

He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”

Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”

Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.
It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.
The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.
“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.

articles.title: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer
articles.summary:
PM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft

The UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this…

blocks.text: The UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this year’s record-breaking summer saw devastating blazes across the country.

The country experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires that triggered an emergency alert to mobile phones in England and Wales. Figures released on 8 October showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.
The Met Office found that the climate crisis made this extreme heat about 130 times more likely.

At the government’s first wildfire resilience summit on Friday, Andy Burnham will announce plans for a new wildfire AI unit in the National Situation Centre, which is part of the Cobra briefing rooms.

Businesses including Google, Airbus and VodafoneThree are expected to attend the summit to set out how satellite monitoring and early warning systems can help fight fires. The government said its new AI unit would enable it to “spot and fight fires faster”.
The prime minister will also announce £45m for fire crews to buy wildfire-specific personal protective equipment (PPE).
This comes after the Guardian revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire PPE.

They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.
Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.
Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.
The prime minister will also announce that military planes and helicopters will be made available to fight wildfires on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said: “As the threat of wildfires in the UK grows, defence will step up to provide greater support to our emergency services and protect military training areas across the country.”

The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high. In August, Burnham announced a temporary ban on sales of disposable barbecues. He has also been criticised for failing to address the climate emergency in his wildfire response.

Farmers will also be given funding to make landscapes more resilient to fires. This announcement comes after the government quietly scrapped plans announced under the Conservative government to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires.

This revelation led Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee, to raise “serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground”.

The government also said it would allocate £25m to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they hold more water and act as natural firebreaks, as well as provide financial support for farmers to fireproof their land.
This new grant scheme is expected to run from April 2027 to April 2029.

Environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole said: “For decades, wealthy grouse moor owners have drained our peat bogs, turning them into a tinderbox. This grant will help reverse that destruction, but must be followed by a new round of landscape recovery funding, and duties on landowners to repair the damage done. It’s time to make England wet again.”

The prime minister said: “I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything. I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs.
“Crews will now have the kit they need to stay safe and military aircraft will stand ready to help tackle wildfires from the sky. We cannot put people through another summer like this one.”

Indian Registrar tells senators she had no choice but to make ‘corrective actions’

Guillaume St-Gelais Dubé trembled and wiped away tears, his voice breaking, as he told a Senate committee earlier this week what it was like to learn last year he’d been stripped of his Indian status by the federal government.
“It's difficult to have that trust in the government after a situation like that,” St-Gelais Dubé told senators.
“It's like your skin is being ripped from your body,” he said.
St-Gelais Dubé is among over 700 members of the Innu First Nation of Essipit who lost their status after a decision by the federal Office of the Indian Registrar.
Guillaume St-Gelais Dubé trembled and wiped away tears as he testified before a Senate committee about being stripped of his Indian status. (Senate of Canada)

The Senate hearing Tuesday was the first time federal bureaucrats from Indigenous Services Canada publicly explained their decision, which was puzzling and devastating for many in the community — located in the Côte-Nord region, about 150 kilometres east of Saguenay, Que.
Indian status entitles community members to land for houses and fishing camps, as well as health and other social benefits.

items: Over 700 Innu community members in Quebec stripped of status take Ottawa to court

blocks.text: Now 700 people are at risk of losing their homes and benefits, as well as their very sense of identity.
“Come to our community, you'll see who I am, what my identity is,” St-Gelais Dubé told senators.
“An identity is not a piece of paper."
Long journey to status
The 738 people affected are all descendants of Christine Kichera and Adelaïde Matshiragan — two Innu women who lived in the 1700s.
For years, they and their descendants were not considered Innu in the eyes of the government because Kichera and Mathshirigan had married non-Indigenous men.
Under earlier provisions of the Indian Act, Indigenous women who married non-Indigenous men lost their status and could not pass it on to their children.
St-Gelais Dubé and many others in the community grew up without status, even though they were raised with Innu culture and traditions.
That changed in 2019 when amendments to the law addressed the long-standing gender-based discrimination.

items: Carney government is stalling on Indian Act reform bill, advocates, lawmakers charge

blocks.text: St-Gelais Dubé and other descendants could then apply for status, which he received in 2023.
“When my status was recognized, it was an enormous relief. I felt liberated to finally have my own identity,” he said.
He was given land by the band council to achieve his dream of building his own house with money he’d saved for years.
But all that came crashing down a year later.

In 2024, he and other descendants of the two women received registered letters informing them their status was under review and that they had 120 days to provide historical proof of their eligibility.
A final decision issued Nov. 5, 2025, revoked the status of the two women and their descendants, effective immediately.
For now, the Essipit Innu band council does not intend to evict those affected and has given them three years to regularize their status.
An 'obligation' to take action, registrar says
Defending the federal government's decision during the hearing were Lori Doran, director general of individual affairs for Indigenous Services Canada, and Claire Thie, the Indian Registrar.
Thie’s job is to validate and review Indian status requests.
Doran told senators the review process began in this case when someone applying for status contacted the Office of the Indian Registrar about the status of their application.
“Through the course of reviewing and preparing a response to that applicant, the source evidence was called into question,” Doran said.
Federal bureaucrats Lori Doran and Claire Thie defended their decision to revoke status from more than 700 Innu before a Senate committee in Ottawa this week. (Senate of Canada)
That source evidence was a late 18th-century record cited known as the Catalogue général de toute la nation montagnaise.
Compiled by a missionary, the document lists members of the Innu community at the time, including Kichera and Matshiragan — but its validity has been called into question.
The Office of the Indian Registrar considered that document to be legitimate when it initially granted status to St-Gelais Dubé and the other Innu in 2023.
But Doran said that was an error.
“The individual that made the initial entitlement decision ought to have escalated this particular application for the registrar to get involved directly," she said.
Thie said when this situation was brought to her attention she had doubts, and was required by law to investigate further.
“We have a strong team of genealogists, researchers as well as subject matter experts, and we don't take these decisions lightly,” she said.

“We worked on this family for a year before we notified individuals. And we were unable to find any additional primary, very solid evidence that would help us ensure that the registration was sufficient under the Indian Act,” she testified.

items: Ojibway man's human rights complaint against Indigenous Services Canada might not proceed

blocks.text: She said in the absence of that evidence, she had no choice but to revoke the descendants' status.
“I have an obligation. I have a duty. I have no choice but to make corrective actions when they're brought to my attention,” Thie testified.
“It may sound cold. It may sound unsympathetic, which I'm not. That's the reality of working in this role,” she said.
Court challenge
Lawyers working for St-Gelais-Dubé and other community members told senators that the people affected were being asked to prove something that was almost impossible.
Lawyer Audrey Mayrand told senators that the reserve in that area was only created after Kichera and Matshiragan died, so their names wouldn’t appear on any official government list.
Another lawyer who’s worked on such cases, Ryan Beaton, said he still didn’t understand why the position of the registrar had changed.

“You have people in this situation who’ve gone through the process, have given the documents, they've been assessed by one registrar as sufficient, they get registered, they remake their lives,” Beaton said.
“And then for reasons that are extremely unclear, we have this kind of new burden imposed on them and they have seemingly no opportunity to possibly meet it,” he said.
Mayrand and other laywers are challenging the decision in Federal Court and the case is ongoing.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Steve Rukavina has been with CBC News in Montreal since 2002. In 2019, he won a RTDNA award for continuing coverage of sexual misconduct allegations at Concordia University. He's also a co-creator of the podcast, Montreapolis. Before working in Montreal he worked as a reporter for CBC in Regina and Saskatoon. You can reach him at stephen.j.rukavina@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Emmy-winning actor Tom Skerritt, with roles in Alien and Top Gun, dies at 93
articles.summary: Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV’s Picket Fences or the doomed captain of…

image.caption: Actor Tom Skerritt, pictured in Burbank, Calif. on February 5, 2018, has died at the age of 93. (Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV’s Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien, has died. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 22, 2026 5:00 PM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure — whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien — has died. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices," the statement said.

Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for Picket Fences, winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights included playing Shirley MacLaine's patient husband in The Turning Point, Sally Field's husband in Steel Magnolias and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in Contact.

From left, Tom Skerritt, David E. Kelley, creator of Picket Fences, and actor Kathy Baker after the show won best drama series during the 45th annual Emmy Awards in Pasadena, Calif., on Sept. 19, 1993. (Douglas C. Pizac/AP Photo)

"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.

Onstage, he was the narrator in Our Town at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's A Time to Kill, in which The Associated Press wrote that he "nicely pulls off a charming, disgraced and drunken lawyer."
Skerritt's early life
Skerritt grew up in a middle-class family in Detroit. His father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child.
He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by Citizen Kane.

His performance in a Los Angeles theatre production of The Rainmaker led to his first film role — a supporting part as a sergeant in the scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film War Hunt in 1962. The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

Redford and Skerritt had been vying for the same lead role, with Redford winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, cast Skerritt in A River Runs Through It, as the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times praised his "halting, thoughtful manner."

items: Robert Redford, Hollywood icon and director, dead at 89

blocks.text: Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."
Alien and Top Gun

The cast of Alien poses on set. From left, actors John Hurt, Veronica Cartwright, Tom Skerritt, Yaphet Kotto, Sigourney Weaver, Harry Dean Stanton and Ian Holm are pictured in 1979. (Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation/Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
After War Hunt, Skerritt struggled for screen time, landing a small role in M*A*S*H and Thieves Like Us for Robert Altman, and a bit part as a motorcycle cop in Harold and Maude for Hal Ashby.

Things changed with The Turning Point, which earned him a National Board of Review award. Then came Alien, with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct while hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea."

Then came another memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark Top Gun: "Gentlemen, you are the top one per cent of all Naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."

items: Top Gun: Maverick is the most Tom Cruise film ever
The first flight of Top Gun (and two other reasons to visit the cinema) in 1986

blocks.text: Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in Picket Fences, a drama created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — including one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.

Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, who played his doctor wife, in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place of bizarre happenings, including a robber who left a trail of frogs and the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.

"It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'"
Tom Skerritt with his wife Julie Tokashiki in Geneva, Switzerland in 2012. (Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for IWC)

On the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's Brothers & Sisters, Jimmy Ford on TNT's Leverage and the recurring character Evan Drake on Cheers. He starred in the Hallmark movie What the Deaf Man Heard, alongside Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modelled for Guess jeans.
Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie Divided by Hate.

"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."
He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

articles.title: Poland: Thousands protest for more abortion rights
articles.summary: Thousands rallied across Poland to demand abortion rights six years after a landmark court ruling tightened restrictions. The country has one of the strictest abortion rules in all of Europe.

image.caption: This protester holds a placard reading 'Let it be the Law! Not a compromise'Image: Mladen Antonov/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands of people took part in abortion-rights demonstrations across Poland on Thursday, including in the capital Warsaw and more than 20 other cities.

Abortion is legal in Poland only when the pregnancy is the result of a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it endangers the life or health of the mother. As a result, most abortions are carried out secretly.
The protesters held placards with slogans such as "Women's hell continues” and “Men of quality don't fear equality."

Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power in 2023 after pledging to loosen Poland's abortion restrictions. But disagreements among members of his governing coalition have hampered efforts to change the law, and protesters have accused the government of breaking its promise.
What is the current legal framework?

Abortion has been legal in the overwhelmingly Catholic country since 1993, but only in cases involving a threat to the mother's life or health, a pregnancy resulting from rape or incest, or severe fetal abnormalities.
In 2020, under the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, abortion laws were tightened even further, and abortions in cases of fetal abnormalities were banned.
Activists say tens of thousands of abortions take place outside hospitals each year.

Women who undergo secret abortions, for instance by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility. However, people who help them, including doctors and family members, can potentially be prosecuted and face up to three years in prison.

blocks.caption: Thousands braved the rain to call for the decriminalisation of abortionImage: Mladen Antonov/AFP

blocks.text: Activists question government’s reform push

The protests on Thursday came just days after Poland’s parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions but which are expected to be vetoed by the country’s President Karol Nawrocki, a politician with the backing of the conservative PiS opposition.
"These are breadcrumbs," Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women Foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, told news agency AFP.
The activists said that passing the draft laws one year before the next parliamentary election was a token gesture with no chance of passing into law.
They accused the liberal Tusk government of merely creating the impression of taking action because it needed women's votes in the upcoming election.

Aisha Zaman, from the Hyson Green area of the city, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.
A weapon was recovered and a large crime scene cordon put in place around Angel Row in the heart of the city after the incident at 4.50am on Sunday.
Nottinghamshire police said the officer was approaching two suspects when he was hit by a bullet. He remains in hospital receiving treatment.

articles.title: Canada Post starting weekend parcel delivery in Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa this fall
articles.summary: Canada's national mail carrier says it plans to start delivering parcels on the weekend to seven million households by the end of 2027, as part of the financially troubled Crown corporation's major…

image.caption: A Canada Post employee returns to a delivery depot in Vancouver following a month-long national strike in December 2024. The corporation says it's starting to see signs of recovery as customers return following years of uncertainty. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's national mail carrier says it plans to start delivering parcels on the weekend to seven million households by the end of 2027, as part of the financially troubled Crown corporation's major restructuring.
Financially troubled Crown corporation gives update on restructuring
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 22, 2026 3:44 PM EDT | Last Updated: 13 minutes ago
Canada's national mail carrier says it has begun delivering parcels on the weekend to homes in Ottawa and Montreal, with plans to expand to Toronto in late November.
The financially troubled Crown Corporation also says it plans to provide weekend delivery to other urban centres like Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary next year.
It aims to offer weekend delivery to seven million households by the end of 2027.

Private carriers have successfully outpaced Canada Post by offering weekend and evening delivery for years. Until recently, the Crown corporation had said it was unable to do the same because of the previous collective agreement it had with its mail carriers.
Senior leadership provided an update on Canada Post's restructuring efforts and finances during its annual public meeting on Thursday.
Canada Post continues to lose money, including $482 million in the first half of 2026 before tax. Leadership said they expect the company will still need to rely on federal loans to stay afloat.

Canada Post employees and supporters rally at Canada Post headquarters in Ottawa during the November 2024 national strike that completely shut down mail service in the country. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

"The continued reliance on government funding is not a long-term solution and we are committed to reduce the reliance on government support as quickly as we can," said Rindala El-Hage, Canada Post's chief financial officer.
Despite the continued losses, Canada Post is showing signs of early recovery, El-Hage said, as customers return after a long period of labour disruption.
Parcel revenue grew by 20.7 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. Operating costs also declined by $119 million.
The Canadian Union of Postal Workers (CUPW) and the corporation signed a new collective agreement in June which stays in effect until 2030.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Marina von Stackelberg is a senior reporter at CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. She recently worked in Berlin as a recipient of the 2026 Arthur F. Burns fellowship. She covers national politics with a focus on health, labour, and the NDP. Marina previously worked as a reporter and host in Winnipeg, with earlier stints in Halifax and Sudbury. Connect with her by email at mvs@cbc.ca or on social media @CBCMarina.

articles.title: Canadian diplomats based in U.S. advised to avoid appearing with midterm candidates
articles.summary: The government of Canada has issued advice to all embassy and consulate staff to avoid appearing with U.S. midterm candidates, according to a source with knowledge of the notices.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford participate in a joint news conference on Wednesday. Both were asked about recent accusations from U.S. officials that Canada is potentially meddling in the midterm elections. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The government of Canada has issued advice to all embassy and consulate staff to avoid appearing with U.S. midterm candidates, according to a source with knowledge of the notices.
Global Affairs Canada says issuing advice to diplomats around elections is routine
Two separate notices were sent out in the last month, the source said.
Those instructions, which Global Affairs Canada describes as routine, come as Trump administration officials level accusations of "potential interference in U.S. elections" at Canadian officials.

In addition, the source said the government told diplomatic staff to be careful with their social media, not pick sides and not pose for photos with candidates. Bloomberg first reported news of the government notices.
The source characterized the advice as basic reminders.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown

blocks.text: "As part of regular business, Global Affairs Canada provides instructions to its Canadian missions abroad. Government officials are always instructed to limit public events and stakeholder engagement during election periods in their host country," a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada separately told CBC News.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" on Wednesday that lists a number of instances it alleges could amount to "potential" interference, including a reference to Bernadette Jordan, Canada's consul general in Boston, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates last week.
Carney, Ford respond to Trump administration's election interference claims
The source told CBC News that the most recent bulletin was sent out last week before the U.S. Embassy issued its statement.

The embassy statement came after two Trump administration officials — trade adviser Peter Navarro and U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra — warned Canadians not to get involved in the U.S. midterms.

Hoekstra specifically mentioned Industry Minister Mélanie Joly in his comments on potential meddling. Four of the nine instances listed in the embassy release also reference Joly's comments about Canada's counter-tariff strategy, going back to March 2025 when she was in charge of foreign affairs.
Joly has pushed back on assertions that she's trying to influence the midterms and did so again on Thursday, saying she has met with both Republicans and Democrats during recent trips to the U.S.
"That is diplomacy, that's what we do," she told reporters during a news conference in Toronto.
Minister denies U.S. election interference claims by Trump administration
The embassy's recent release also mentions the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Regan ad that ran in the U.S. last year and comments made by Premier Doug Ford.
Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.
"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."
Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."
"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.
Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms
The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates in border states like Michigan and Maine.
The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.
"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Katie Simpson and Kate McKenna

articles.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
articles.summary: As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

image.caption: The response to Albania's protests has turned increasingly violentImage: Olsi Shehu/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.
Why Albania's political crisis is deepening
Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."
She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

blocks.caption: Anti-corruption protester "Sara" says communication occurs onlineImage: Kristi Çavo/DW

blocks.text: Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

blocks.caption: A protester hurls back a tear gas canister fired at students by policeImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."
Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

blocks.caption: Arlind Qori says the protesters are voicing legitimate demandsImage: Kristi Çavo/DW

blocks.text: "People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.
"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
articles.summary: Lina Attalah, who is accused of managing a website without a license, will go to court next week. Mada Masr has published reporting critical of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

image.caption: Lina Attalah, born in 1983, has years of journalism experience in Egypt and was previously the managing editor of the Egypt Independent online newspaper before the closure of its print edition [File Photo: 2020]Image: Khaled Desouki/AFP

blocks.text: Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution sent Mada Masr journalist Lina Attalah to stand for trial, the independent Egyptian news website said Thursday.

One of Madr Masar's co-founders, Attalah serves as the site's editor-in-chief. The website, which publishes in both Arabic and English, frequently features critical reporting related to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.
What do we know so far?
Prosecutors questioned Attalah for six hours on Wednesday in New Cairo, Mada Masr said.

She is accused of running a website without a license and the publication of false news "with the aim of disturbing public peace." Under questioning, the latter allegation was dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.
The trial has been referred to a New Cairo misdemeanors court and is slated to begin on October 27.
Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr's legal counsel, said there was "haste" in the trial referral and said the trial beginning next week signals "unjustified urgency."
Al-Azhari said Attalah could face a financial penalty of between 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (around €16,000 to €48,000; $18,000 to $54,000) if convicted.
Mada Masr said the organization has sought a license from the Egyptian government to run its news website since 2018 — the same year Egypt passed and ratified a law to regulate the press.

Egyptian authorities have been unresponsive over the past years to Mada Masr's attempts to procure a license, with Mada Masr later finding out in 2022 that its request was rejected. The site filed a lawsuit in 2022 and found out in 2023 that the rejection was due to missing documents.

The proceedings against Attalah come after Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists last month for independent fact-checking and investigative website Matsadaash (Egyptian Arabic for "don't believe").
Press freedom groups condemn actions against Attalah
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed alarm about Attalah's referral to trial.

"Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns in years, which began with the arrest of the six Matsdaash journalists," the CPJ's director for Middle East and North Africa Sara Qudah said. "It is long past time for Egypt to end this campaign and allow independent media to report freely."
Reporters without Borders (RSF) had earlier said it was alarmed by prosecutors' questioning of Attalah.

According to RSF's World Press Freedom Index, Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries, with many of the country's biggest news outlets either state-owned or controlled by wealthy businessmen who submit to the will of the government.

Egyptian President el-Sissi came to power in a 2013 military coup against Islamist President Mohamed Morsi. Since then, el-Sissi has cracked down and blocked websites such as Qatar's Al Jazeera and The New Arab on allegations of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.

articles.title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
articles.summary: Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are at risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change the biggest threat. A new study found that 96% of reef systems are critically endangered.

image.caption: Australia's Great Barrier Reef is among those threatened Image: Norbert Probst/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.
In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.
Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.
Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

blocks.caption: Coral reefs are home to a high level of biodiversityImage: Yuddy Cahya Budiman/REUTERS

blocks.text: What are the threats to the reefs?
Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).
Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.
This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.
Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.

When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.

blocks.caption: Sea turtles are among the animals that depend on coral reefsImage: Great Barrier Reef Foundation/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the reefs still be saved?

"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.
"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.

"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

articles.title: Meta board placates Zuckerberg after threat to leave California if voters approve wealth tax measure
articles.summary: Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg, Reuters has reported, in a move spurred by a California ballot measure, part of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, that has sparked heated debate and…

image.caption: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg listens to U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on Sept. 29 in Washington, D.C. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg, Reuters has reported, in a move spurred by a California ballot measure, part of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, that has sparked heated debate and hundreds of millions in campaign spending.
Polls suggest a tight result on Prop 40, as some tech barons threaten to move out of state if it passes

Under the deal, Zuckerberg will get non-voting shares he can sell to potentially foot a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event the proposal is ​approved, in exchange for a commitment to remain a ​resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday.

Zuckerberg, the world's sixth richest person ​according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence ⁠outside California because Proposition ⁠40, the ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth ‌tax," could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.

Proposition 40 asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5 per cent tax on the state's billionaires, and needs over 50 per cent support to pass. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth upwards of $2 trillion US.
State health care programs would be the biggest beneficiaries of proceeds raised through the fund, with money also going to state food assistance programs and public education.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign

blocks.text: The parent company of Facebook and Instagram said Zuckerberg needs to continue to manage the company from its Menlo Park headquarters at a time of "unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry." Meta says it needs to ⁠raise "hundreds ⁠of billions of dollars" over several ​years to ​finance its AI-related growth ⁠plan.

Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027. Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of ‌about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20 per cent of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10 per cent of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill from Prop 40 without losing voting control.
Brin equates tax to Soviet-style oppression

Backers say California's measure would generate $100 billion US for health care, food assistance and education. But skeptics peg the revenue estimate at closer to $40 billion US and say it could also drive some billionaires ‌out of ⁠the state, depriving California of future tax revenue and investment.
Sergey Brin, Google co-founder, has spent more than $100 million US to defeat the ballot measure.

"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don't want California to end up in the same place," Brin recently told the New York Times.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin is shown on Oct. 8 during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C. Brin has spent millions trying to defeat California's Proposition 40 ballot measure. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Darien Shanske, a law professor at the University of California-Davis, who helped draft the proposal, told CNBC that relocating wouldn't limit the tax exposure of the ultra wealthy. Any billionaire residing in the state on Jan. 1, would still be taxed, given the state's tax laws, he said.
Prop 40 is supported by, among others, California Democrat Ro Khanna in the House of Representatives and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

"Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?" Sanders said at a rally in California earlier this month.
LISTEN | The latest on the midterms from our Washington correspondents:
Two Blocks from the White House34:00What Trump's very bad week might mean for the midterm races
Passage of the measure far from certain
The measure hasn't elicited a tidy split of progressives and Democrats in favour versus billionaires against, however.
Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, for example, has shrugged off the proposal.

"The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang told CBS News earlier this week. "I feel it's a privilege. It's a responsibility. And nothing would give me more joy than to be able to pay even more taxes."
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, seen at a Los Angeles campaign stop on Oct. 15, doesn't believe Proposition 40 is an adequate way to fund state services. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Meanwhile, outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes Prop 40 and backs the Brin-introduced Proposition 42, which would seek to amend the state constitution to ban such tax proposals after Jan. 1, 2026.

Newsom's position earned a rebuke from outspoken actor Mark Ruffalo, who called it "beyond sad" on social media. Messaging directly to Newsom's account, Ruffalo said Democrats need someone who is "tough when it comes to the real imbalances people are struggling with every day: billionaires vs. people and the planet."

But current Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and the California Teachers Association (CTA) are also among the individuals and groups opposed to the measure, arguing that while well-intentioned, it is a complex and unsustainable funding measure. The CTA is focused on Proposition 3, which would raise funds through a state income tax hike on high earners.
Becerra's Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, is staunchly opposed to Prop 40.

items: Trump's complaints of 'rigged' L.A. mayoral vote could offer preview of midterm election night

blocks.text: California voters have only approved one in three citizen initiatives historically. As well, California ballot measures typically need robust early support, political analysts say, as history has shown the undecided are more apt to choose No when it comes to time to vote.

"California ballot measures tend to lose support over time, and if it's polling below 50 per cent in August, that's not a good sign for its prospects," John Pitney, a ​professor of politics at Claremont McKenna College, told Reuters in a report published Sept. 30.
A Citrin-Politico poll released this week indicated that, of those who took a position, 46 per cent of survey respondents favoured Prop 40 while 43 per cent were opposed.
With files from Reuters and the Associated Press

articles.title: 'Looksmaxxing' influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
