blocks.text: A woman told police that on 23 May 2025, Peters ordered her an Uber to his family's house in Chatham where they were drinking alcohol while filming a livestream before he allegedly raped her, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
The police officer who took the report said he believed she was unable to consent due to her age and the level of intoxication she exhibited in the livestream, CBS reported.
Clavicular has more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and has garnered media attention for extreme measures he has taken for "looksmaxxing".

He has admitted to using a hammer on his face and jawline and taking a number of steroids, injections, and other drugs to achieve bodily perfection. He also gives advice on appearing masculine and performs stunts to shock followers.
In Florida earlier this year, he was charged after filming himself shooting at what appeared to be a dead alligator. He pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public.
In March, he was arrested on suspicion of battery after authorities suspected him of instigating a fight between two women. Authorities said in July that they did not intend to file charges.
After Thursday's hearing, Peters posted a photo of himself in the black suit and black tie he wore to court, while holding his dog which he also brought to court.
His next hearing will be on 24 November, when the judge will decide if there is enough evidence for the case to move forward.

articles.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
articles.summary: Websites were taken offline after the developers of programming language PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" had been discovered.

blocks.text: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.
Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.

"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

articles.title: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest
articles.summary: A Ukrainian man was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia - one of several such cases in Germany this year.

blocks.text: Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.
Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".

Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".
He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.
In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.
Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.

articles.title: Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
articles.summary: It's the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" as Canada seeks to diversify trade beyond the US.

image.caption: The leaders of Canada and Turkey announced a new strategic partnershipImage: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a two-day visit to the Mediterranean country.
During the visit, Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Turkish presidential palace in Ankara.
Erdogan: A 'new era' in Turkey-Canada relations
The two leaders announced that the Canadian-Turkish relationship would be upgraded to a "strategic partnership," covering areas such as trade, energy and people-to-people ties.

"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both of our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said alongside Erdogan.

Erdogan said we "are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," while hailing Carney as a leader with "common-sense and acumen." The Turkish leader said negotiations on a free trade agreement with Canada will begin before the end of 2026.

"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion (€2.6 billion), to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan continued.

blocks.caption: Turkey has a bigger military than Canada and is a global leader in drone productionImage: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canada and Turkey, both members of the NATO military alliance, agreed to deepen their defense relationship during the visit.
Canada seeks to diversify trade relationships amid Trump tariff onslaught
The Canadian prime minister, a former central banker, is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday in Istanbul.
Carney's visit comes as Canada seeks to broaden its trade relationships with other countries beyond its southern neighbor. Nearly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States.
Since reentering office in 2025, US President Donald Trump escalated a trade war against Canada and imposed tariffs on many Canadian goods, leading Canada to wean itself off the US.
Turkey has a population of over 86 million people and the world's 16th-largest nominal GDP as of 2026. Canada, meanwhile, has a population of over 41 million people and the 11th-largest GDP.
Amnesty tells Canada: Emphasize human rights in negotiations with Turkey

Carney's visit to Turkey also comes as Erdogan and his conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP) crack down on the opposition and critical media. In addition, the Turkish government has targeted the LGBTQ+ community with mass arrests.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown
Ruhat Sena Aksenir, the Turkey director of human rights watchdog Amnesty International, said: "Canada must not treat human rights as secondary in the negotiations."
"Sustainable partnerships depend on accountability and respect for the rule of law," she continued.
The AKP has ruled Turkey since 2002, with the party, and particularly Erdogan, consolidating power.

According to human rights organization Freedom House, Turkey is "not free" and scores low in the areas of political rights and civil liberties. Reporters without Borders ranks Turkey 163 out of 180 on its World Press Freedom Index.

articles.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
articles.summary: The Brazilian president accuses the tech firm of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro, which it denies.

blocks.text: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.

In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.

It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".
The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.
Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".
He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.
Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots? Ask our Europe columnists
articles.summary: At 3pm BST / 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct, Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in…
articles.byline: Rokhaya Diallo, Alexander Hurst, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1d agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation

blocks.caption: The Hôtel de Ville in Limoges, central France, on fire during a weekend of unrest. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors, resulting in a debt sell-off, with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.

The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”

Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”

And the Guardian’s editorial noted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”

What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in which France finds herself?

France-based Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST on Friday 23 October to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.
Comments will open at 0900BST on Friday, but you can send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com

articles.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
articles.summary: Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave in 2021.

blocks.text: A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.
In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.
The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.
Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.
On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".
The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.
Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary.

articles.title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
articles.summary: Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy is airing the ad featuring her mother, whose husband was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.

blocks.text: Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable".
Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday evening, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done".

In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.
Since it launched on Monday, the ad has generated political backlash and cast a national spotlight on the race.
Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.
In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.
"I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening.
"You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad.
According to information provided to the BBC by Acton's campaign, the last time she saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted.
Arthur's husband fled town before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004.
In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.
Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.
The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".
On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.
"And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."
MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.

articles.title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage

Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was…

blocks.text: Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.

Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.

The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.
Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.

It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.

The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.
The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.
The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.

AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.
The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.

blocks.caption: Lawyers for Sasan Ghandehari said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information. Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/Alamy

blocks.text: The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.

Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”
He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.

The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.

Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.
after newsletter promotion
The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.

According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.
In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.

Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.

Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.

In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.

It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.

In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.

blocks.caption: The Picasso painting at the centre of the court case was Femme dans un rocking-chair. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images

blocks.text: At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

articles.title: France's Macron says 'illegitimate' protests will be banned in coming days
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are…

image.caption: Some students took to the streets of Paris again on ThursdayImage: Teresa Suarez/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that demonstrations organized by groups without legitimate authority would be banned in the coming days.
Over the past weekend, protests over the education system and the cost of living escalated into violence and looting, which the government blamed on ultra-left groups.

"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysee Palace with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers.
"The general recommendation is not to hold demonstrations in the coming days," he explained. "We want calm to return."
Macron said the ban on protests aimed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed," he added.
Fresh demonstration in Paris

In the wake of the past weekend’s violence, several cities had already implemented curfews for certain parts of town. Protests planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned from going ahead.
Authorities say a massive security operation was planned for the coming weekend to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence.

blocks.caption: The historic city hall in Limoges was set on fire and partly collapsed on October 17Image: Elise Cabane/PHOTOPQR/Populaire du Centre/MAXPPP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Student and university groups as well as unions have said they would continue to mobilize and hold protests. On Thursday, thousands gathered in Paris when a local court was said to have overturned the day's demonstration ban.

France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook the country in 2018 and 2019, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.
France: Why students are taking to the streets
What are the protests about?
The protests started in September at a school near Paris over lack of funding for the education system.
The demonstrations then spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually to other French cities. They have since widened to also address the soaring cost of living and deteriorating public services.
On October 17, the protests escalated into the worst urban unrest in years when masked rioters clashed with police, looted shops and set cars and buildings on fire.
Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on the 19th-century Limoges city hall, French media reported.
Across France, there were around 2,700 arrests last weekend and hundreds of protesters, police and firefighters were injured.
French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said courts jailed 217 people in fast-track trials linked to rioting over the weekend, adding "this figure is continuing to rise a lot."
Macron on Thursday said talks between authorities, student groups, unions, and employers would take place on Monday. He stressed that dialogue over protesters' legitimate demands should continue.
The unrest comes just months before next year's presidential election, in which voters will choose Macron's successor.

articles.title: Meta strikes deal to stop Mark Zuckerberg leaving California over billionaire tax
articles.summary: The Meta boss had said he would exit the state over a wealth tax that has not yet come into force.

blocks.text: Meta has agreed a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to stop the Facebook co-founder from leaving California after he threatened to move from the state because of a proposed tax on billionaires.
The agreement allows Zuckerberg - reportedly one of the world's richest people - to sell shares in Meta without losing control of the Californian-based company if he needs to pay a large tax bill.
The measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on state residents with a net worth of more than $1bn (£750m), is yet to pass. Californian residents will vote on 3 November.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg secured a deal with a special committee at Meta after "robust", and "at several points, contentious" negotiations.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
Zuckerberg - who has a $226bn fortune according to Forbes' billionaires tracker - had told Meta's board that it was his intention to remain with the firm for "the foreseeable future".

However, he said he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and, if he listed his home on the real estate market, it "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees".
This, he told the board, "would raise questions for management of the company going forward".

A special committee within Meta decided it was "critically important" to keep Zuckerberg in a leadership role and in California to manage the firm from its headquarters "during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry".
Tech companies in the US and globally are spending billions of dollars on developing artificial intelligence and the infrastructure around it.
Meta said the share deal was appropriate to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely" with the company's AI at its headquarters.
It said his "talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the special committee wants that to continue".

articles.title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
articles.summary: The attack on the unidentified victim follows a wave of anti-migrants protests in South Africa this year.

blocks.text: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.

According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.

The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.
Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.

The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.
One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.
Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.
These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.
Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month.
Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals.
His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated.
One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic.
"We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.
The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.
Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.
Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.
Additional reporting by Pumza Fihlani in Johannesburg

articles.title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
articles.summary: As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

image.caption: The French police has used tear gas, rubber bullets and stun grenades against protestors Image: Sylvain Thomas/AFP

blocks.text: Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
France's protests grow

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

blocks.caption: Some tools used by the French police are banned or rarely used in other  countries Image: Manon Cruz/REUTERS

blocks.text: Weapons made for war?
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
France: Why students are taking to the streets
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Confrontation vs. de-escalation
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

blocks.caption: Police arrested protesters in the German town of Lützerath, but with less force than at similar protests in FranceImage: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: When can police officers use force?

According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

articles.title: OSG seeks hold on use of 2026 appropriations
articles.summary: Government lawyers have advised the Marcos administration to put on hold the implementation of some programs in this year’s national budget as they prepare to appeal a Supreme Court ruling…

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Government lawyers have advised the Marcos administration to put on hold the implementation of some programs in this year’s national budget as they prepare to appeal a Supreme Court ruling declaring the 2024 and 2025 outlays and parts of the 2026 budget unconstitutional.

Solicitor General Darlene Marie Berberabe said the government wants to clarify some aspects of the high court ruling, specifically the guardrails prescribed for the exercise of budgetary powers, as these could affect the execution of projects.
She noted that the ruling bars the executive branch from touching Special Provisions 1-a and 1-b of Chapter XLII of the 2026 budget, which pertains to the release of unprogrammed appropriations.

According to the Supreme Court, the provisions are unconstitutional since the budgetary ceiling imposed under the Constitution applies to the total of both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations. The Constitution states that Congress may not increase the total appropriations recommended by the President.

“Our advice to the DBM (Department of Budget and Management) and the executive branch is to withhold for now (the implementation of some programs in the 2026 budget) since we expect it to be decided upon immediately,” Berberabe told a media briefing yesterday at Malacañang.
“Our Supreme Court will surely prioritize this because the Supreme Court does not want the execution of the budget to be affected,” she added.
However, the solicitor general believes that the projects in the 2026 budget covered by the high court ruling but whose implementation started before it was issued should continue.
Berberabe said she is scheduled to meet with Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon on Monday to discuss the programs to be affected by the court decision.
At a Senate hearing yesterday, De Leon said no releases have been charged against special provisions of the unprogrammed appropriations (UA) in the 2026 national budget.
“The releases from the 2026 UAs are only for FAPs (foreign assisted projects),” De Leon said.

He assured lawmakers that the department is prepared to work closely with Congress in reviewing and refining the relevant budget provisions, while coordinating with the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) on legal questions arising from the SC decision.
“We commit to work with the Senate and Congress to fine-tune the special provision for unprogrammed appropriations,” he said.
Deadline for appeal
The OSG has until Nov. 4 to appeal the ruling, according to Berberabe.

“The implication is the 2026 budget will be affected. But we believe it will be seen once it is reassessed. We will appeal and explain the effect. We understand the guardrails, in fact, there is no issue there... We will show why no constitutional requirement or standard was violated,” Berberabe said.

While acknowledging that safeguards are essential to ensure transparency, accountability and fiscal discipline in the use of public funds, the OSG said there is a “complex challenge” in distinguishing safeguards required by the Constitution from those whose formulation falls within the powers of Congress and the executive.
Asked whether there was a possible overreach in the Supreme Court’s decision, Berberabe replied: “That is one of the things we are looking at.”

“The OSG believes that the Constitution bestowed powers – power of the purse is for Congress; the power to prepare the budget and to propose to Congress, that’s for the executive. After the passage of the GAA (General Appropriations Act), the executive handles the execution of the budget,” she added.
According to Berberabe, it was not the first time the budget passed by Congress was higher than the figure in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) proposed by the President.

She said it also happened in 2000 during the administration of Joseph Estrada, in 2004, 2008 and in 2010 during the presidency of Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and in 2022 during the leadership of Rodrigo Duterte.
Valid tool

Former Senate president Franklin Drilon, meanwhile, lauded the SC’s recognition of unprogrammed appropriations as a valid budgetary tool, but urged Congress to seek clarification on portions of the decision that may encroach on its constitutional authority over budgeting.

Based on his reading of the decision, Drilon said the SC affirmed that unprogrammed appropriations are not unconstitutional per se, as they provide standby spending authority that may be exercised only when funding conditions prescribed by law are met.

He said seeking clarification is appropriate because the ruling, as currently written, may go beyond constitutional review by prescribing fiscal conditions that, under the 1987 Constitution, should be left to the best judgment of Congress. Drilon said the ruling affects Congress’ authority to determine appropriations.
Drilon also said the SC ruling comes at a crucial stage in the preparation of the 2027 national budget. “We look forward to seeing how the reforms will be reflected in the 2027 budget,” he said.

As amicus curiae during the proceedings, Drilon acknowledged that flaws or abuses in the use of unprogrammed appropriations may require correction. But the standards needed to address them should be expressly imposed by Congress through legislation, with the court determining whether those standards comply with the Constitution.
“Congress determines appropriations and their lawful conditions. The executive implements the budget within those conditions. Both functions remain subject to the Constitution,” Drilon said.
Replacing the funding trigger enacted by Congress, he warned, could narrow legislative discretion and restrict the executive’s ability to implement the budget under the approved framework.
“The concern therefore extends beyond one administration or one budget. It involves the scope of the budget powers available to future Congresses and presidents,” he said.- Aubrey Rose Inosante

articles.title: Alcantara’s ex-aide confirms flood cash deliveries
articles.summary: A former personal assistant of disgraced Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) district engineer Henry Alcantara confirmed that he delivered billions of pesos’ worth of alleged…

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am
Former Bulacan 1st Disrtict engineer Henry Alcantara attends the House Infra Comm's first hearing on anomalous flood control projects on Tuesday, Sept. 2, 2025.
House of Representatives / Released

MANILA, Philippines — A former personal assistant of disgraced Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) district engineer Henry Alcantara confirmed that he delivered billions of pesos’ worth of alleged kickbacks from flood control projects to fugitive former party-list congressman Zaldy Co from 2022 to 2024.

Alcantara’s former personal assistant Wirt Walter Rosales testified for the prosecution at the continuation of the hearing for the bail petition in the plunder case against former House speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez before the Sandiganbayan Third Division yesterday.
Rosales’ sister is the live-in partner of Alcantara, and he got to work with him in 2021 after his seafaring career was halted at the onset of the pandemic.

Rosales recalled he delivered plastic storage boxes containing cash to Co’s residential units at Horizon Homes at Bonifacio Global City in Taguig thrice in 2022, and seven times at the former lawmaker’s residence along Ladybug Street in Valle Verde 6 in Pasig City from January 2023 to December 2024 using suitcases.

The medium suitcases could contain up to P20-million cash in bundles, while the large ones could be stuffed with up to P30 million, according to him. He noted the amounts could increase between P5 million and P10 million if the suitcases made of cloth could be expanded.

Rosales noted Alcantara joined the deliveries, but when the cash-filled packages were sent to Horizon Homes, Alcantara would stay at the coffee shop while Rosales was the one carrying the packages from the basement to Co’s alleged two units on the 56th floor.

While Rosales claimed he did not see Co in all the deliveries, Co’s alleged aides John Paul Estrada and Mark Ticsay would sign “acknowledgment receipts” prepared by him and Alcantara’s staff and engineer Carlo Rivera, during times when Alcantara did not join the delivery. The receipts were later thrown away upon Alcantara’s instruction.
Included in the receipts were separate sheets of paper indicating the project and the percentage of the kickback, which were left to Estrada and Ticsay.
The cash-stuffed packages were prepared beforehand at a “secret room” inside Alcantara’s office at the DPWH Bulacan 1st District engineering office, according to Rosales.
When asked where the money came from, Rosales said he was not sure if it came from project contractors since he heard it from Rivera.

Rosales said that he and Rivera counted the cash by bundles and, once put in the storage boxes and suitcases, the money would stay in the “secret room” overnight. Rosales recalled that the cash could have amounted to at least P200 million at times.
When pressed by the Sandiganbayan justices how much in total could he have delivered to Co, Rosales maintained he was “not sure” but it could have reached more than a billion pesos.
Also presented during yesterday’s hearing was police Major Ermelo Dichoso Jr., one of Co’s former security officers from January 2024 to May 2025.
He confirmed that he knew Co’s other security officers previously part of the Marines, who earlier testified about deliveries of cash-stuffed suitcases.

He added he accompanied Co in four instances where he had meetings with fellow lawmakers at the Aguado residence in Manila, at the Manila Polo Club Townhouses and at Romualdez’s two houses on Tamarind Road and Narra Avenue in Forbes Park.
However, he maintained the meetings and what he called “special taskings” – wherein cash disguised as “garbage” were disposed of or delivered – were separate events.
The court scheduled the next hearing on Oct. 27, where Rivera would be presented as one of three prosecution witnesses.

articles.title: NBI: P3.5 billion shabu from Laos points to Philippines network
articles.summary: The foiled smuggling of 521 kilograms of suspected shabu valued at P3.5 billion from Laos demonstrated how huge the Philippines’ drug market is and the sophisticated system that attempted…

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am

Ross Jonathan Galicia, who heads the NBI’s Dangerous Drugs Division, told House lawmakers their investigation indicated a local distribution network was behind it, with enormous resources, huge funds and networks that cross boundaries.
PNA / File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The foiled smuggling of 521 kilograms of suspected shabu valued at P3.5 billion from Laos demonstrated how huge the Philippines’ drug market is and the sophisticated system that attempted ttransport such volume by air, an official of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said yesterday.

“There is a local crime group that is operating within the country. It would take a number of people to move these illegal drugs. There’s a big market in the Philippines,” he said during a probe conducted by the House committee on dangerous drugs.
Galicia likewise said investigators must look beyond the drugs intercepted at Luang Prabang International Airport on Oct. 1 and examine the network that would have received and distributed them.
“Destination is the Philippines. We have established that,” he said, adding that those behind the operation had the funds to charter an aircraft and move the shipment quickly.

Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) director-general Isagani Nerez told the committee that they, along with the Philippine National Police, were building a case against individuals allegedly involved in financing, arranging and receiving the shipment.
The PDEA chief said investigators were gathering transaction documents covering the aircraft charter and seeking official investigation records from foreign counterparts.
The Bureau of Customs, however, said its own records had not yet established a Philippine recipient or importer.

Deputy Commissioner for intelligence Emmanuel Luis Licup reported that Customs found no notice of arrival for the aircraft and was still awaiting aviation, customs and investigation documents requested from Lao authorities.

“No verified Philippine consignee identified,” Licup said, presenting the bureau’s assessment. “The alleged Philippine destination remains under validation pending receipt of documentary evidence from foreign counterparts.”

The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines also reported that an entry and exit permit had been requested for the aircraft, but the flight was never activated and the aircraft did not enter Philippine airspace.
Intensified search

Police have intensified their search for former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang and four other people who snubbed subpoenas for them to shed light into the P3.5-billion shabu shipment from Laos.
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. has ordered police to find Rimbang, who was tagged as the financier of the foiled drug smuggling operation.
Rimbang, Abdulah Karim Macalatas, Abdullah Rimbang Macarimbang and Aldren Samante did not show up for the probe being conducted by the police Criminal Investigation and Detection Group.
For Nartatez, Rimbang and the other persons’ participation are necessary to establish the complete circumstances surrounding the drug shipment that was intercepted by Laotian authorities on Oct. 1.
The CIDG is wrapping up its probe and will submit a report of its investigation to Nartatez as early as today.
“The evidence gathered reflects a thorough, evidence-based approach aimed at establishing the truth and ensuring accountability,” he said.

The CIDG has issued over 40 subpoenas to persons and companies, reviewed CCTV footage and examined documents linked to the attempt to transport large quantities of illegal drugs using chartered aircraft. – Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Health promotion budget cut flagged
articles.summary: Former Department of Health secretaries have expressed alarm over the drastic budget cut to the DOH Health Promotion Bureau, warning lawmakers that it is a violation of the Universal Health Care Act.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am

From the proposed P2.5 billion, the HPB’s 2027 budget has been reduced to P485 million, or 0.18 percent of the DOH’s total budget, in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 general appropriations bill.
BW FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Health secretaries have expressed alarm over the drastic budget cut to the DOH Health Promotion Bureau, warning lawmakers that it is a violation of the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act.

Section 30 of the UHC Law states that “the cost of implementing health promotion programs shall be at least one percent of the DOH’s total budget appropriations, ” the Healthy Philippines Alliance (HPA) stressed.

“Slashing funding for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases will ultimately cost the government far more in secondary care and emergency hospitalizations in the future,” said Jaime Galvez Tan, former health secretary and HPA lead convener.

“Diabetes, heart and kidney disease and hypertension are overwhelming Filipino families and draining our health care system. Prevention is our most cost-effective tool and we urge Congress to restore and expand funding to protect public health,” he added.

Filipino families, especially those from low-income households, lose the support and resources they need to protect them from preventable risks when the budget for health promotion shrinks to P400 million, former health secretary Esperanza Cabral said.
“It strips the poor of their right to services that can save their lives. We cannot protect vulnerable communities when HPB is severely underfunded,” Cabral said.

Former health secretary Manuel Dayrit said, “A budget cut of this scale undermines the mandate of the UHC Law. It is counterproductive to our goal of achieving a financially sustainable universal health care, which is fundamentally guaranteed to every Filipino.”

articles.title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
articles.summary: Raghad and Raad's family had to flee their home on foot because of the fighting between pro-government forces and the Houthis.

blocks.text: Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages
ByOrla Guerin
Senior International CorrespondentReporting fromAden
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.
They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.

When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.
What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.

"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden

blocks.text: The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden
As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.
Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.
The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says

blocks.text: More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says
Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.
The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.
Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.
The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.
The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.
Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina

blocks.text: Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina

We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.
"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."
Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.
"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."
Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.

Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition

blocks.text: Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition
As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.
There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.
That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.
"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.
"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."
A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.
Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment

blocks.text: Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment
The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.
"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."
They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.
"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."
She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street

blocks.text: Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street
Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.

As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.
So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

articles.title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate‘ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
articles.summary: French president will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ regarding demonstrations on Friday as part of tough security response to recent rioting

blocks.text: Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.

Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.

Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but may have to use alternative routes.

The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”

blocks.caption: Macron attended the security council meeting at the Élysée Palace on Thursday as he sought to restore calm. Photograph: Suarez Teresa/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the Republic”.

“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was later overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for that day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.
after newsletter promotion

Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of the Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.

Authorities in Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.

However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.

blocks.caption: A demonstration involving members of the gilets jaunes on the capital’s Place de la Republique on Saturday. Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big city mayors later in the day.

The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Elysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.

The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections that will choose Macron’s successor.
