articles.title: France confirms first Shamonda virus infection in a human death of 'severely immunocompromised' individual
articles.summary: The Shomonda virus has been detected in a human for the first time, French health officials said. Authorities see no risk to the public, adding that the victim, who died in early October, was…

image.caption: French health officials say the livestock virus poses no theat to the public, pointing out that the first detected human infection was an exceedingly rare caseImage: Alexis Jumeau/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: French health officials on Thursday confirmed that they had detected the Shamonda virus in a human — who died early this month — in what they say was the first-ever case of a human contracting the livestock disease.

"Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," said France's Ministries of Health and of Agriculture in a joint statement.
"No health risk to the general public identified at this time," they said, adding that the human infection appeared to be, "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient."
How is Shamonda virus transmitted?

First ​identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the insect-borne Shamonda virus is a variant of the Orthobunyavirus, a genus that contains 138 species, and primarily affects livestock, ‌particularly cattle.
It is transmitted by culicoides, or biting midges.
The virus has been detected in ​animals in Africa and Japan for years and has been spreading across Europe this year.
Until now, it was not thought to be transmissible to humans.

According to a press statement on the Ministry of Agriculture's webpage, "At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the case resulted from vector-borne transmission via the bite of a culicoid midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was reported to be circulating among animals in the spring and summer of 2026."

The ministry said biological, clinical and epidemiological investigations are being carried out by experts in human, animal and environmental health, adding that authorities at the World Health Organization and European Center for Disease Control had been notified of the incident.

articles.title: ‘Justice is hope’: Here are Leonen’s 9 promises as aspiring chief justice
articles.summary: 'Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer.... On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,' says Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

blocks.text: LEONEN. Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen during the Judicial and Bar Council's public interviews for chief justice candidates on October 22, 2026.
Supreme Court of the Philippines
'Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer.... On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,' says Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

items: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen presented nine promises aimed at enhancing the Philippine judiciary as he seeks to become the 28th chief justice.
Leonen emphasized the importance of an independent judiciary and the need for the court to serve the marginalized, promising to uphold accountability and accessibility in the justice system.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen gave not one, not two, but nine promises on Thursday, October 22, as he vies to become the country’s 28th Supreme Court (SC) chief justice.

Leonen was the first of five candidates to face the Judicial and Bar Council for its public interviews. Leonen said his plan includes a promise to enhance the expertise of judges and ensure that justice is accessible to everyone — especially the marginalized.

items: Improvement of judges Continuation of Unified Legal Aid Service (mandatory free legal service of lawyers), developmental and social change lawyering, program of remote hearings and translation. More exposure for judges to jails and communities “Judges at every level must remain open to the possibility that their premises are mistaken,” Leonen said.

Transparency in resolving cases When a case is submitted for decision, Leonen said the parties should be told the date by which the SC is expected to decide on it. If the date won’t be met, the parties should be told why.

Continued digitalization of courts Leonen said the entire justice system should be digitalized — from the Department of Justice’s prosecution, trials at regional trial courts, to the appellate courts and SC.

Accountability in public office Quicker resolution of corruption cases “Every case already filed by the Office of the Ombudsman arising from large-scale corruption decided at first instance before the end of 2027, the horizon of our Strategic Plan,” Leonen said.
Consultation with business sector Review of regulatory actions and reporting of alleged exactions or extortions by any court official or employee

Creation of more courts Leonen said at least 10 halls of justice should be built in the country’s poorest provinces. “Where no building will ever be close enough, our court will travel, as it did from Bongao to Simunul, Tawi-Tawi,” he added.
Court’s independence If he becomes chief justice, Leonen said the SC will publicize any attempts at interference, who the court officials and employees met, about what, and what was asked.

Creation of laws for those who need it Review Batas Pambansa Bilang 129 and consolidate the Rules of Court and the special rules into a Philippine Code of Pleading and Practice. Rules on the customary law of the indigenous peoples Writ of Kalayaan, which will compel “agencies responsible for a detention facility to act on its conditions, together and in the open”
A review of the legal profession Review on the admission to the Bar Improvements for Shari’ah (Islamic law) counselors and lawyers

blocks.text: Leonen said he will continue Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo’s plan to innovate the judiciary.

“I offer all these, with my faults and weaknesses, which I constantly try to overcome. The ideas we debate today and the personalities who will appear before you pale in comparison to this: our people still suffer,” the aspiring chief justice said.

“Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer. Yet they still come to our courts, holding their folders and their receipts, because they have decided that this is where their grievance belongs. On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,” he added.

blocks.caption: ‘Justice is hope’: Here are Leonen’s 9 promises as aspiring chief justice

blocks.text: Leonen said that in these times of political and economic challenges, the Philippines needs a chief magistrate who is independent and ready to make hard decisions for the people.

He believes a chief justice should protect the confidentiality of SC deliberations, encourage other justices to speak up about their opinions, explain the Court’s decisions fully, and protect dissent.

“All this because the judiciary should be where government is held to its conscience, the Constitution. A judiciary beholden to powerful interests — past, present, or future — does not deserve its name,” the senior magistrate said.

Leonen said he will be, if ever, an independent chief justice, as proven by his track record. He said he has been senior associate justice for nearly 14 years and has worked with 5 chief justices and 37 associate justices.
According to him, he has been an acting chief justice on many occasions and has chaired the SC’s 2nd and 3rd Divisions, among others.

“I have voted, on principle, against the legal positions of the President who appointed me, and of every President who has sat since. I have also written unanimous decisions that clarified the framework and limits of the discretion of powerful departments and officials in government,” Leonen said.
“I do not say this to my credit. It is the only assurance worth anything to the public,” he added

Leonen said the court’s success will be measured by whether the poorest litigants can rely on it, if they can tell their families the justice system gave them a fighting chance in a case. He also believes that court decisions should reach and be understood by everyone.

The chief magistrate added that lawyers should think of empowering people. As officers of the court, Leonen said they should explain what the law is, why the law is the way it is, and what could be done about it.

“Justice is hope. Hope is honored when a remedy is owed to a named person, by a date, and then delivered. Anything short of that reduces hope to a mere sentiment. Our people have been offered sentiments for a very long time,” Leonen said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Grandparent hugging consent ad pulled after criticism
articles.summary: Jim O'Callaghan described the video as "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".

blocks.text: The Irish minister for justice has criticised an advertisement produced by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) promoting consent, calling it "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".
The ad depicts two grandparents enthusiastically hugging a young boy, but when they approach their granddaughter she appears unhappy about the exchange.
It includes the message "not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them".
The ad, which has since been removed, has attracted criticism and and also received international coverage in publications such as the New York Post.
Fianna Fáil politician Jim O'Callaghan, whose department funds the campaign, said the the video has since been removed following engagement with the DRCC.
He said the video "does not represent the views of the Government".
"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them.
"While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."
The video was part of a campaign titled 'We-Consent', which is led by the DRCC.

In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said: "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.
"We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too.
"We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have."

As well as the Department of Justice, the 'We-Consent' campaign is also supported by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, and CUAN (the Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Agency).
All three have been approached for comment.
Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill said the video was a waste of resources.
"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said.

"The issue of consent is a very serious one and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children.
"But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark."
He added: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said: "'We-Consent' is a programme created and developed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, aimed at informing, educating, and engaging the public about all forms of consent.
"Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low-cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign.
"The Department understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review."

image.caption: Iranian military forces are present in the southeastern border region Image: Farhikhtegan

blocks.text: Recent weeks have seen renewed attacks, assassinations and armed clashes in the southeastern province bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. The incidents occurred in the provincial capital of Zahedan, as well as smaller border towns.

The border region of Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan is home to the Baloch ethnic minority. The region on either side of the Iran-Pakistan border is among the most economically disadvantaged of the wider area.
The Pakistani province of Balochistan is economically underdeveloped, despite having large reserves of natural gas, gold and copper.

The situation is similarly dire in the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchistan, which is predominantly inhabited by Sunni Baluchis. It is one of the poorest regions in the country and marked by underdeveloped infrastructure, limited educational opportunities and water supply shortages.
Significantly less information is available about the situation of the Baloch in Afghanistan.
Armed groups sense security gaps
Various Baloch groups are active in Iran and Pakistan, some of whom seek Balochistan independence. Yet to date, there is no evidence of coordinated cross-border cooperation among these organizations.

In December 2025, several Baloch opposition groups in Iran united under the umbrella of the Popular Fighters Front. Observers see this as an attempt to more closely integrate their political and military activities.
This coalition, which formed before the outbreak of the Iran war, could try to exploit security gaps created by the current situation, Iranian journalist Mehdi Nakhl Ahmadi told DW.
Ahmadi, who lives in Italy, has been covering the situation of the Baloch people for years. He said the new security situation could allow armed groups to expand their operations.
Struggling with poverty, suffering marginalization

Ahmadi said there are structural reasons for Baloch dissatisfaction. "The Islamic Republic's security policy toward ethnic and religious regions has widened the gap in economic development between these regions and other parts of the country in recent decades," he said.
He added that the rising number of attacks points to a shift in dynamics, as do increased coordination and changes in the way recent operations have been carried out.
Among the victims of recent clashes were members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the Basij militia, armed individuals, and a Sunni cleric.

A source within Iran, who is familiar with the situation of the Baloch people, yet whose identity we cannot disclose security for reasons, attributed some of the armed violence to political, economic and religious discontent.
Discrimination in employment, education, regional development and religious matters contribute to the tension, the source said.
Hidden executions surge in Iran during US-Israeli war

That's why the armed conflict should not be viewed in isolation, the Iranian source explained. Clergy, academics and other social leaders had been trying for years to peacefully voice their demands for better social policies and greater investment in the region, the source said.
The fact that these efforts were largely unsuccessful had led to a growing willingness among some to resort to more radical measures.
"The high number of executions in recent decades is another factor that fuels discontent," said the source. Most documented executions in the province, meanwhile, are related to drug offenses.

Although Baluchis make only up an estimated 2–6% of the Iranian population, they are significantly overrepresented among those put to death. Iran Human Rights reports that Baluchis accounted for 9% of all recorded executions in 2025. In previous years, that figure was 11% (2024) and 20% (2023), respectively.

For many people who live in this economically disadvantaged region, smuggling opium into Iran, and fuel out of the country, are one of the few ways to earn a living. This, in turn, has contributed to a continued military and security presence at the border.
It is not, meanwhile, known whether armed groups in southeastern Iran are being supported from abroad.

blocks.caption: For many people in the region, fuel smuggling across the Iran-Pakistan border is one of the few ways to make a livingImage: Abdula Ghani Kakar/DW

blocks.text: Violence has also escalated in the Pakistani province of Balochistan. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, 131 armed attacks were recorded there in September, up from 89 in August.

In addition to the separatist movement, which has been active for years, the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) are also expanding their operations. This had led to strategically important transportation links between Iran and Pakistan coming under growing pressure.
Still, it cannot be said with certainty whether the recent uptick in violence in Iran's Sistan and Baluchistan province stems from security gaps resulting from the Iran war.
The growing number of attacks does, however, suggests that the security situation in the already fragile border region continues to deteriorate.
Additional reporting by Morad Rahmati.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Carney announces trade and defence partnership with Turkey
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, walks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as he arrives at the Bestepe Presidential complex in Ankara, Turkey, on Thursday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence co-operation.
PM visits Ankara seeking stronger ties with key NATO ally
It is the latest step in the warming of relations between the two nations and an important moment in the prime minister's plan to co-operate more closely with other middle-power countries.
Carey praised Turkey as an "exceptional" partner.
"No country builds strength alone," he said in a joint statement at the sprawling presidential palace compound.

"The most resilient countries bring together complementary strengths with trusted partners. Our goal isn’t self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience. That’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for Canadians."
There are four pillars to the new partnership — trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and people-to-people ties.

Next month, negotiators will sit down in Ankara for the first round of free trade talks. Also, the partnership includes a new agreement on defence industry co-operation that will better connect Canadian and Turkish companies.
Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, seen here in Ottawa on July 16, will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The partnership will also pave the way for investments in the energy and critical minerals sectors. The two countries will also finalize an air transport agreement, increasing passenger flights between the two countries.

The bilateral visit, a first for Canadian prime minister, comes as human rights groups raise the alarm over Turkey's sweeping crackdown last month on dissent and civil society groups, including the dismantling of 2SLGBTQ+ and HIV-advocacy organizations.

"The prime minister has been very clear. We need to engage with the world as it is, not the way we wish it to be," Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said ahead of the trip. He will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials.
People run from the police during a march in support of transgender people and their rights during the 2SLGBTQ+ Pride week, in Istanbul, Turkey, on June 21. (Dilara Acikgoz/The Associated Press)
"Where we have differences of opinion, we discuss those in private."

Carney is looking to diversify Canada's trade to make the country less dependent on the United States. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific.

Turkey, a member of NATO with a growing defence industrial sector, is seen as a key ally on the trade and military production fronts, says Thomas Juneau of the University of Ottawa, an expert in the Middle East.
"What the Carney government appears to be making as a choice is not to restrict diversification efforts only to democracies, only to countries that have positive human rights records," said Juneau.
Turkey has become increasingly authoritarian under Erdogan, who has been president since 2014.

"This is morally a difficult dilemma on the Canadian side, but the calculus appears on the part of the government that if Canada were to choose to diversify only with democracies the ceiling for success would be low."
Immediately after landing in Ankara on Thursday, visited Anitkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who was the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey.

The structure and its 750,000 square-metre grounds are beautifully maintained, divided into the Peace Park with tens of thousands of plants and trees including Canadian maples, and the Monument Block. Carney laid a wreath at the monument.
Carney pays his respects after laying a wreath during a ceremony at the Anıtkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, in Ankara. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Turkey aims to expand its energy capacity significantly in the coming decades, planning to add roughly 20 gigawatts of nuclear power by 2050.

To that end, Ottawa and Ankara are reportedly planning to set up a working group to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's Candu nuclear team in order to build Turkey's planned second or third nuclear power plant.
Hodgeson declined comment on the possibility.

items: Carney's Turkish balancing act must include business, defence and human rights
Turkey's president gifted Carney a revolver at NATO summit. Carney gave him maple syrup

blocks.text: Sevag Belian, the executive director of the Armenian National Committee of Canada, says any nuclear deal with Turkey deserves close scrutiny.

He pointed to the previous falling out between the two countries which resulted in Canada imposing a de facto arms embargo, which was mostly lifted in 2024. The lifting of those measures was the price Erdogen demanded of the Trudeau government for getting behind Sweden's membership in NATO.
The fallout started in 2020 when Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to importation of Wescam target acquisition gear used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.

"We know from the disclosed documents that they had said that they will be using the few cameras that they got through the exemption for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria," said Belian.
"But then we know that those cameras were actually diverted illegally to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno.
"We have established through parliamentary investigation that the Turkish side clearly lied."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk
articles.summary: As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation…

image.caption: Tetjana, a local resident in Sloviansk, couldn't afford leaving the city even if she wanted toImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: A few days ago, three Russian aerial bombs struck a residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Sloviansk. One hit a five-story apartment building, injuring seven people. Along with neighboring Kramatorsk, Sloviansk is one of the last major towns in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. Since summer, the city has been a combat zone.

In a courtyard surrounded by damaged apartment blocks, a dusty carpet hangs over the metal frame of a swing set. Tetjana, a pensioner who lives in the building across the street, has brought it out of her rubble-strewn apartment to clean it. She was in her kitchen when the bombs struck.
"The bomb hit the second floor, and a woman who lived on the fourth floor was screaming," she tells DW. "They managed to rescue her before that entire section of the building collapsed," she adds.

Despite being offered the opportunity to evacuate, Tetjana has yet to leave Sloviansk. "I don't know where I would go," she says. Rent can cost up to €400 ($449) a month. Tetjana's pension is the equivalent of just €67 ($75) a month. Even with monthly relocation assistance of about €40 ($45), she could not make ends meet. "I couldn't live on that. Nowhere!"

Meanwhile, electricity and water are still available in her neighborhood, but the gas supply has been cut off. "We'll get through this," Tetjana says hopefully. "Everything will be OK. That's what I tell everyone. I want that so much."

blocks.caption: People who want to evacuate are not allowed to bring their pets Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Residents reluctant to evacuate without pets

Days after the attack, the few residents remaining in the damaged buildings were still clearing out their apartments. But another attack hit as they worked. This time, the bombs struck a building housing a state-run emergency assistance center and the Red Cross. While firefighters put out the blaze, rescue workers and volunteers retrieved belongings left inside and cleared away broken glass. Eight people were injured in the attack.

"I was on the balcony when there was a deafening bang. It felt as if someone had hit me over the head," says Natalja, describing one of the recent attacks. The pensioner comes to this part of the city to care for her twin sister. "She can no longer get around. Today, I couldn't bring her bread, only crispbread," she tells DW. Although shops and a few stalls remain at the burned-out market, bread is not available every day.

blocks.caption: Volunteers help clear the debris and retrieve belongings from a resilience center after a Russian bomb struck the building in SlovianskImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "I tried to persuade my sister to leave. I would go to a nursing home and she would go to a hospital. But her dog is sick, and I have one, too," Natalja says, noting that pets are not allowed during evacuations. "I can't leave my sister behind. She is worried and angry with me, as if everything were my fault. I have no strength left."

Natalja slowly sets off for home, "so I can get there before dark." The city center is nearly 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) away. Public transportation has been suspended since 30 people were killed in an attack on two buses in neighboring Kramatorsk.

blocks.caption: Natalja cares for her twin sister who refuses to leave as she would have to leave her dog behindImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "We're used to living under fire"

The center of Sloviansk is heavily damaged. Few people are out on the streets, though a handful of shops remain open. Of the city's 100,000 residents, about 20,000 remain, most of them elderly people who are unable to leave.

Vasyl, a pensioner, is from the village of Mayaky, north of Sloviansk. A neighbor drove him into the city center, where he sat down for lunch in a cafe. "We're used to living under fire by now," he says. "But it's a bad habit. We should have broken it long ago."
Vasyl wants peace for his homeland. But he rejects Russian President Vladimir Putin's demand that the part of the Donetsk region under Ukrainian control be handed over to Moscow.

blocks.caption: Life has almost come to a standstill in Sloviansk and only few shops and market stalls remain openImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Two elderly women talk on a street covered with nets to protect against drones. "I can't remember the last time I slept through the night," says Iryna, a pensioner. "It's terrible, but I have nowhere to go. I'm supposed to leave my two cats behind, but I love them so much. They're all I have."
"We can only hide, trembling, and pray to God that everything will be all right," Iryna continues. "When I have to go to the market, I don't know if I'll make it there alive."
Russian drones attacked the central market several weeks ago, injuring at least three people. Since then, fewer vendors and customers have been coming to the market.

blocks.caption: The constant buzz of drones and the fear of Russian attacks keeps people from sleeping through the nightImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "We dream of staying here"

Valeriya sells women's underwear. With kindergartens closed, she has to bring her 5-year-old daughter Sofia to work. Their neighborhood in Sloviansk is not yet subject to the mandatory evacuation of families with children.
"We're used to this life by now. We were evacuated in 2022, but later returned. Now we're waiting to be evacuated again," Valeriya says.

Sofia races through the market aisles with her friend Anya, who is a year older. Anya's mother is a soldier defending her hometown. Her grandmother, Tetjana, sits nearby selling men's clothing. She, too, has to look after her granddaughter while working.

blocks.caption: Sofia, 5, and Anya, 6, play at Sloviansk central market as their kindergartens are closed due to the warImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Tetjana has started shipping her belongings to the Dnipropetrovsk region, where she hopes to start a new life. She is sending them while the post office is still open. "It hurts to see our Ukraine being destroyed," she says, fighting back tears. "Who will rebuild our cities?"

She hopes to return one day. But the fate of Bakhmut weighs on her mind. "Look at Bakhmut. There are no houses left. I'm counting on our boys to hold our cities, even though it's very difficult." Bakhmut, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Sloviansk, fell to Russian forces in 2023 after months of heavy fighting.

The women see little hope for a ceasefire. "Putin won't want one. And our younger generation will ask us what we fought for in the first place," Tetjana says. She believes Russia must withdraw from Ukrainian territory.
Drones buzz overhead as gunfire echoes across the market. "It's hard for our boys to shoot them down," Tetjana says. "But they're doing their best."
Russian strikes hit civilians in Ukraine
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
articles.summary: The suspect is thought to have gathered-defense related information for Russia.

image.caption: The suspect is expected to be brought before a judge on FridayImage: Uli Deck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in the German state of Brandenburg have arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said Thursday.

The man, identified only as Vadym Y. by prosecutors, is suspected of having used his connections to European defense firms to gather information that he then allegedly passed on to a Russian spy agency.
Prosecutors said he had been in touch with a middleman since July 2025. They said he had been gathering intelligence in connection with the Russian invasion of Ukraine from Germany.

This information reportedly included "details regarding the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO's eastern flank"

Germany has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months, especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.

articles.title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
articles.summary: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.

Yemeni Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.

Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.

The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, who also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.

Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.

Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf.

However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.
after newsletter promotion

Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.

articles.title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
articles.summary: The deaths include two women found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

blocks.text: At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.

In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."

articles.title: Alex Eala bows out of Ningbo Open after loss vs Diana Shnaider
articles.summary: Shnaider says she is happy with her performance against Eala, referring to the Filipina tennis ace as a 'dangerous and tough opponent'

blocks.text: FRUSTRATED. Alex Eala in action for the Philippines at the 2026 Singapore Open.
WTA/Ashok Kumar
Shnaider says she is happy with her performance against Eala, referring to the Filipina tennis ace as a 'dangerous and tough opponent'
MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala conceded to sixth seed Diana Shnaider, 5-7, 4-6, at the round-of-16 match at the Ningbo Open on Thursday, October 22.
Eala had looked to secure a back-to-back win at the Ningbo Open after earlier defeating France’s Diane Parry in straight sets in the round-of-32 game on October 19.

blocks.caption: Alex Eala kicks off Ningbo Open campaign with win over Diane Parry

blocks.text: “It’s definitely much better than my previous one,” World No. 13 Shnaider said about her performance against Eala. “I’m obviously very happy the way I played today because, definitely, Alex is a very dangerous and tough opponent.”
Both players are left-handed, and Shnaider had referred to the Filipina tennis ace as a “big hitter” she knew would be challenging to beat.

“It’s never easy to play another lefty…. I feel like you gotta just get used to the ball. The first few games, you just kind of get used to the spin, where is her strike zone, what is her weakness. You just gotta give yourself a little bit more time to adjust, and then it becomes a little bit easier when the game goes on,” the Russian player said, explaining her technique in the match against Eala.
After defeating Eala, Shnaider secured her spot in the last eight and will face the US’ Iva Jovic in the quarterfinals of the Ningbo Open.
The 21-year-old Filipina had previously made an early exit at the Wuhan Open after absorbing a loss from World No. 177 Shi Han of China in the round of 64.
Eala is currently ranked World No. 20. – Rappler.com

articles.title: House opposition urges Senate to address 'illegal' provisions of 2027 budget
articles.summary: Opposition lawmakers in the House of Representatives have asked the Senate Finance Committee to address the "illegal" provisions of the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed national budget for 2027…
articles.byline: LLANESCA T. PANTI, GISELLE OMBAY, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 7:14pm

Opposition lawmakers in the House of Representatives have asked the Senate Finance Committee to address the "illegal" provisions of the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed national budget for 2027 if the House leadership won’t recall its approval.

House Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio of Alliance of Concerned Teachers party-list and Assistant Minority Leader Renee Co of Kabataan party-list made the call in the aftermath of the Supreme Court decision declaring the 2024, 2025 and portions of 2026 national budget unconstitutional.
Likewise, the Supreme Court ruled in the same decision that lump-sum appropriations under the said national budget in various years that have no clear purpose are unconstitutional.

Tinio and Co cited that the House-approved 2027 budget has illegal provisions based on the Supreme Court ruling that came out two days ago, such as the P50 billion Armed Forces of the Philippines modernization fund and P42 billion Financial Assistance to Local Government Units, which are lump-sum amounts.

“Our call is for the recall of House Bill 10858 (proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for 2027). Kung hindi po ito gagawin ng House, the last opportunity para matanggal ang mga illegal provisions ng 2027 GAB (General Appropriations Bill) for now ay sa Senado o kaya naman po sa bicameral conference committee (bicam),” Co said in a press conference.
(If recall won't be done, then this should be addressed by the Senate finance panel or the Bicameral Conference Committee.)
The bicam reconciles the House and Senate versions of the proposed national budget.
“Malinaw na kailangang umaksyon ang Kongreso para maging compliant sa Supreme Court decision. Kung hindi, muling maidedeklarang unconstitutional ang ibang bahagi ng budget for 2027,” Tinio added.

(It is clear that Congress needs to act to make the 2027 budget compliant with the Supreme Court ruling. Otherwise, the Supreme Court will declare portions of the 2027 national budget unconstitutional again.)
In response, Senate Finance panel chairperson JV Ejercito said that the House recalling its third reading approval of the national budget is not the solution at this point.
“Ako, I am worried on that kasi kapag ginawa ‘yun, most likely, hindi tayo papasa, mukhang hindi natin maipapasa by year-end ang budget. Kasi very tight na,” Ejercito said in an ambush interview.
(I’m worried about that because if that happens, it’s highly likely that we won’t be able to pass the budget by year-end because the timeline is already very tight.)

Ejercito also cited several factors that may affect the budget timeline should the House GAB be recalled, such as the upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Meetings and the resumption of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
He thus suggested that disagreeing provisions of the proposed 2027 budget be reconciled during the bicameral conference committee meetings instead.

“Sana sa bicam na lang natin ayusin ito kung saka-sakali. Tutal, hindi naman lahat ito…iba na ngayon ang bicam, talagang pinag-uusapan na hindi na tulad dati. Wala ng small committee. At least, we're transparent, lahat naman ito will be televised,” Ejercito added.

(Hopefully, we can just resolve this during the bicameral conference. After all, the bicam is different now. There’s no more small committee. At the very least, we’re being transparent and the entire process would be televised.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter
articles.summary: Journalist Will Murray describes how he and a bystander saved an SUV driver from his vehicle.

blocks.text: A man in a sinking car has been saved by a TV journalist after driving into deep flood water.
Will Murray was at the scene reporting for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Morayfield, Queensland, when he saw a vehicle drive past him into the water.
Murray, and a bystander, rushed to help the driver as the SUV sank.
Murray says when it became clear the car was sinking very fast "there was no thinking involved", because the man might have drowned.
"Better that you jump in and give it a crack", Murray tells BBC News.

articles.title: First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
articles.summary: The disease, which usually affects cattle, has been identified in a patient who died in early October.

blocks.text: The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said.
Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public.

Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was monitoring the situation and officials were still investigating how the virus had spread to a human.

It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring.

They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings.
The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill.
"Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia".
Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production.
The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection.

The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey.
The case has also been reported to the World Health Organization.

articles.summary: China is weaponizing not just its commodities against the Philippines, but its own people, according to Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro on Thursday.

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 7:01pm
China is weaponizing not just its commodities against the Philippines, but its own people, according to Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro on Thursday.

Diplomatic tensions between Manila and Beijing have flared after Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan said China would easily win if it used force in the West Philippine Sea, a remark that earned condemnation from many Filipino leaders.

"Dito naman sa ekonomiya, sa araw-araw mong binibili, um-over naman tayo ng asa sa China, at ang China, hindi katulad ng ibang bansa, niwe-weaponize nila ang commodities, pati tao. 'Di ba may threat na 'uy, kung hulihin niyo 'yung mga iligal na ginagawa ng aming kababayan dyan, pauwiin namin 'yung mga OFW (overseas Filipino workers) niyo,'" Teodoro said in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.

(Regarding the economy, with your everyday consumption, we have relied too much on China, and China, unlike other countries, has weaponized their commodities, even people. There is a threat of 'oh, if you catch the illegal things that our countrymen do there, we will send your OFWs home.')

"Kaya pati tao wini-weaponize. Ngayon, ang task ng gobyerno maghanap ng alternatibong markets at saka mag-industrialize ang Pilipinas para sa ganoon kaya natin gumawa, at least at a bare minimum, na ikinabubuhay ng ating bansa na kailangan talaga kasi nagkakaroon ng gipitan ng mga commodities sa mundo," Teodoro added.

(Even people are being weaponized. Now, the task of the government is to look for alternative markets and then industrialize the Philippines so that we can manufacture, at least at a bare minimum, something that our country could live on, which is really needed because of the tightening of commodities around the world.)
Beijing previously apprehended over 100 Filipinos in China for alleged immigration violations, an act that Teodoro had previously called extortion and blackmail.
Teodoro said that there were markets outside of China such as India, which has large-scale production.

While he admitted that it would cost money to change since the country was used to China's supply trade, Teodoro reiterated that it was important to have a wide supply chain so that the Philippines was not overdependent. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: 'Agent Layla': A sex assault victim went undercover to bring her abuser to justice. Now he's out on parole
articles.summary: A parole board decision to release the man who sexually assaulted her has created a whiplash effect for Vienna Luke, who is simultaneously advocating against Justin Sewell’s release from a halfway…

image.caption: Justin Sewell confessed to sexually assaulting his younger sister-in-law in 2007. (submitted by Shawnessy Luke)

blocks.text: A woman who went undercover to get a confession from the man who sexually assaulted her says she's "fed up" and "retraumatized" by a parole board decision to release him.

The parole board decision comes as Vienna Luke has received support from people across Canada and abroad who have heard her extraordinary story of going undercover as an RCMP agent in the CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla.
"I feel deflated," said Luke of the decision to release Justin Sewell early. "My story being out there is like, 'Wow, look.' But there's still so much work to be done."
18 years of fighting for justice. 6 months in prison. 7 months in a halfway house.

The parole board made its decision to release Sewell on Oct. 6, citing his low assessed risk to reoffend and his compliance and participation in therapeutic programs during his time in a halfway house.
Justin Sewell (left) was a trusted brother-in-law to Vienna Luke (second from right) and Shawnessy Luke (right). Vienna met him when she was 10 years old. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
As described in the Personally: Agent Layla podcast and in court documents, Sewell drugged, assaulted and photographed Luke in 2007 when she was 20 years old.

After wrestling for years with what really happened the night she was drugged into unconsciousness and assaulted, Luke decided in 2019 to report the assault to police after she and her sister, Shawnessy Luke, recorded a phone conversation with Sewell's ex-lover who said he disclosed putting ketamine in Vienna's drink. In court, Sewell has denied it was ketamine, but a provincial court judge found it was either ketamine or Valium.

RCMP proposed a plan to put Vienna Luke undercover, giving her the code name Agent Layla. They used emails to entice Sewell to meet her face to face at a hotel lounge at the Vancouver International Airport under the premise that him telling the truth might be a path back to family reconciliation.

In the recording from the sting, obtained by CBC and included in Episode 3 of the Agent Layla podcast, Vienna Luke pushes Sewell to describe the specific details of his offence. He admits to drugging and assaulting her, and to watching her through her bedroom window on two separate occasions.
Eventually, Sewell pleaded guilty to sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism.
Sewell was a successful veterinarian in the northern B.C. community of Fort St. John at the time of the assault. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)

After what was described in court as an unusually lengthy sentencing hearing in which Sewell took the stand arguing that a self-diagnosed addiction to pornography was the root cause of his offences, a provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to two years less a day of house arrest in April 2025.
Seven months later, a panel of B.C. Court of Appeal judges overturned that decision and imposed a sentence of 33 months less a day to be served in prison.
After serving about six months in a federal institution, Sewell was granted day parole and transferred to a halfway house in April 2026.

Since then, according to notifications provided to his victims and viewed by CBC News, Sewell has been granted permission to leave the halfway house and travel to his home in Fort St. John or to "recreate" in Grande Prairie, Alta., for 70 days over a period of less than seven months.
Discrepancies in 2 Parole Board of Canada decisions made 6 months apart

The Parole Board first considered Sewell's applications to be granted full parole in an April 2026 face-to-face hearing. His case was up for review again six months later in early October. This time he was subject to a paper review, a parole decision-making process that assesses documents written about the offender's behaviour and programs they have completed, but does not interview the offender.
The two boards came to a few markedly different conclusions.

The parole board members in April 2026 found in their decision that Sewell "engaged in considerable rationalizing and minimizing" of his offences. Instead of addressing the "key issues leading to your violence," the board found he focused on "[his] use of pornography and the problems in [his] marriage, as though solving those particular problems was a solution also for the behavioural issues that led to the sexual assault."
"The Board believes that a day or full parole release to your home community is not adequate to the task of protecting the community from your risk."

With support of her sister Shawnessy Luke (left), Vienna Luke went undercover in her own case and obtained a confession. The sisters continue to work together seeking justice in the case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Six months later, despite letters from Vienna and Shawnessy Luke imploring the board to weigh heavily the findings of the April board members who interviewed Sewell and decided against full parole, the October parole board members found Sewell's "compliance, community adjustment, ongoing therapeutic involvement, and low assessed risk" support a reduction in supervision and that release on full parole "will not present an undue risk to society."

That board granted full parole on Oct. 6. Correctional Service Canada confirmed the end of Sewell's sentence is Jan. 1, 2028. For the 14 months that remain, Sewell is required to report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with females, and he is prohibited from accessing pornography.
'How is [he] allowed the freedoms to go on a recreational hunting trip?'

For Vienna Luke, it has been an intense time. On the one hand, she's received messages from podcast listeners commending her for sharing her story of confronting her abuser, which led to a conviction and prison time. On the other hand, she's found herself still advocating behind the scenes for justice in her case.
"I'm a person that chose to report," she said. "You can understand why people are just like, 'I'm going to move on with my life.'"

In the most recent parole board decision, board members cited a letter from the Luke sisters questioning the 70 days Sewell was allowed to leave the halfway house, including his release "for the purposes of a hunting trip."

Justin Sewell in a photo where he is hunting. This image is from before he faced the courts for his assault on Vienna Luke. Sewell is now under a 10-year prohibition on possessing firearms. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
The sisters say that in September they began to suspect that some of Sewell's trips might be to participate in hunting, an activity he described as an important hobby in court.

Concerned he might be violating a 10-year ban on using firearms, the Luke sisters say they called the Fort St. John RCMP non-emergency line to alert the police. They say the officer on the line told them Sewell had been granted permission to go hunting with an "approved associate."
Vienna Luke said she met with Correctional Service Canada and parole board officials to express her concerns.
"As they talked and continued to justify how they were handling him ... and their allowances to him, I started shaking. I was so upset," she said.

The sisters weren't worried for their personal safety. They live in Vancouver, about 800 kilometres from Fort St. John as the crow flies. Their concern was that the decision to grant him time to participate in a hobby was at odds with the seriousness of the crime.
"We had a hunch he was going hunting, but we didn't think he was approved to go hunting," said Vienna Luke.
"We were livid," said Shawnessy Luke.

CBC News reached out to Correctional Service Canada to confirm the details of Sewell's permission to go hunting. In an email, it says the organization cannot provide details of travel permits because of the Privacy Act.

The statement adds that "[w]hile we cannot talk about specifics of this case due to privacy, please note that if, at any time, an offender's risk increases or there is a change in their behaviour ... we take immediate action."

The Luke sisters' concerns were summarized by the parole board, who wrote in the October decision: "It is also concerning that your index offence involved violence and yet you are requesting to engage in an extended activity which involves weapons."
Vienna Luke wants systemic change

Vienna Luke knows the outcome of her case – a conviction in a historic sexual assault – is rare. But throughout the lengthy process since she first reported the assault seven years ago, she has found herself questioning whether the justice system is working for sexual assault survivors.
"You would think that maybe the fact he went to jail, he went to a halfway house, the justice system is telling me that I should feel grateful. Look at what you got," she said.
"I feel ungrateful. What did we do all this work for?"
Vienna Luke told her story in honour of other women who have told their stories of surviving sexual assault. (Vienna Luke/Submitted)

In interviews for the podcast and elsewhere, Vienna has emphasized she is telling her story to honour sexual assault victims who went before her. She told their stories, including their struggles with the justice system, which gave her strength in the hardest times.
Now she's receiving emails from other women telling her she has become a symbol of strength for them.

"I've come so far," she said. "To be in a place where I can speak about what happened to me, what was done to me publicly, and everything I did in this process is unbelievable and really I just feel so proud."

articles.title: MovePH trains Movers in Cebu on local reporting, civic organizing
articles.summary: The MovePH workshop brings together Cebu community journalists and civic leaders to design campaigns around underreported community issues

blocks.text: MOVE CEBU. Over 30 Movers trained during MovePH’s roadshow in Cebu at the University of San Carlos , October 15. Photo by Isabella Limbaga
The MovePH workshop brings together Cebu community journalists and civic leaders to design campaigns around underreported community issues

MANILA, Philippines – Dozens of volunteers, among them campus journalists and civic leaders, recently completed MovePH’s two-day workshop at the University of San Carlos Downtown Campus in Cebu City, focusing on reporting on local issues to drive community action.
Organized by Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH and Rappler’s training arm RappLearn, the workshop was part of MovePH roadshow dubbed “#MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa Sugboanon.”
To bridge journalism and advocacy, the workshop’s 35 participants on October 15 and 16 pitched story ideas and advocacy campaigns to address livability issues in their localities.
“Across history, social movements and change have been catalyzed by powerful storytelling,” said Rappler community lead Pia Ranada told participants during the workshop opening.
She cited Rappler initiatives like Project Agos, a citizen reporting platform connecting people in need with rescue and relief agencies, as well as citizens’ reporting of Primewater‘s poor services.
“Narrative is power. Information is power. That’s why powerful people seek to control public stories,” Ranada said.

Rappler managing editor Miriam Grace Go emphasized that effective journalism starts at the grassroots level, urging participants to look at national policies through a local lens, supported by hard data, official documents, and community voices.

“Why do you cover local? The local policies directly affect your daily life, and local is where you are influential,” Go said. “Local is not just an area; local also refers to community. The human stories that interest all of us are those of the communities.
She continued: “National policies are implemented by local governments. Ultimately, localities are the ones affected…. [So] if you want to be an effective journalist, you start local.”

Participants pitched reports on underreported issues, like poor quality constructions along Mandaue City’s Butuanon River, the rise in working minors driven by living costs and parentification, how local carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable, among others.
They drafted preliminary paragraphs, and mapped out paper, electronic, and people trails for how to complete their stories.

blocks.caption: TESTING IDEAS. Rappler editors and community storytellers review participants’ pitches during the revised Movers Program workshop at the USC Downtown Campus on October 15. Photo by Joan Alindogan/Rappler

blocks.text: In the civic action track, participants proposed how to organize public action around community issues. They mapped out campaign objectives, community partnerships, and sustainability plans.

The resulting pitches tackled a range of community concerns across Cebu, like confronting stereotyping of performers with dwarfism, addressing food safety and sanitation at the Colon Street Night Market, documenting displaced families living under a bridge in Minglanilla, training motorcycle delivery riders on safety and income loss during heavy rain, and mounting a student-led HIV awareness and testing caravan.

On the second day, participants presented their campaign plans and opening story drafts to Rappler facilitators and peers for structured feedback, before concluding with a session on using the Muni app to bridge reporting and grassroots community action.

“I grew up on an island with barely any medical support. We would travel an hour on the water to reach the mainland and travel another hour to reach hospitals. When an emergency arises, this inconvenience only adds to the problem,” said Venice Lapingcao Quidato, a participant and Mover from Cebu.
Quidato said when stories like these are published, it does not ask for resiliency, but accountability.
She said attending the MovePH and RappLearn workshops made her realize the importance of developing campaigns rooted in lived realities.
“Narrative building makes people go to the streets, and this is why we need more storytellers and civic leaders in our community,” Quidato said.

blocks.caption: LEVELING OFF. A participant outlines what she hopes to achieve in translating local issues into grassroots reporting and civic campaigns during the opening session of the Movers workshop, October 15. Photo by Felix Olandria/Rappler

blocks.text: For other participants, the training underscored how community-level reporting carries influence far beyond immediate geographical boundaries.

“Our perception of local stories and its impact is not limited to where it is coming from, but the power it holds to birth more stories and ultimately move people to action,” said Joshua Eli Narajos, a Mover from Cebu.
Narajos shared his takeaways in the Padayon Cebu chatroom during the session, saying local stories should never be underestimated.
Movers are expected to work on their story and action pitches in November. They will also receive mentorship and support from MovePH and its partners.
Interested in joining the Rappler Movers’ program? Sign up here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman – US politics live
articles.summary:
Nancy Mace said: ‘This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season’

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoVivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman

blocks.text: Responding to the ad yesterday, Amy Acton told a group of voters that her mother was not well and Ramaswamy shouldn’t have “exploited her”.
Earlier in the week, her brother had called Ramaswamy’s attack ad a “despicable low” in a statement released by Acton’s campaign:

double quotation markIt’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.

double quotation markAfter he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”
The ad, which had circulated among conservatives on social media, featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, urging Ohioans to not vote for her daughter.
The Ohio gubernatorial campaign between Acton and Ramaswamy is regarded as one of the uglier contests in the 3 November midterm elections.
Acton has refused to debate Ramaswamy, who she has called a “chronic liar” and has also criticized him for airing an ad which features a woman married to a registered sex offender.
Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less than two weeks out from the midterm vote and the campaigns are getting even more nasty.

Condemnation continues of Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign in the Ohio governor race after his team put out an attack ad, featuring the estranged mother of his Democrat rival Amy Acton criticising her daughter and calling her a liar.
Acton’s campaign has called it a despicable ad after putting out the clarification that Acton was sexually abused by her stepfather and removed from her mother’s custody at age 12.

Ramaswamy’s team however has dug in behind the ad, and were backed by Veep JD Vance yesterday who condemned Republican criticism. He said Ramaswamy “had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls ​it out like it is”.
However South Carolina congresswoman Nancy Mace joined the chorus of Republican critics saying:
double quotation markThis ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.
She said she was stunned, adding:
double quotation markI just can’t believe that this is what passes for decency in this election.
Stay with us for more developments.

articles.title: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years
articles.summary:
Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions

The son of

blocks.text: The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” the post said. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi, won the 1991 Nobel peace prize, in almost total seclusion for five years after the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing – who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup – was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

articles.title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
articles.summary: Four members of the so-called Gang Suppression Force have been missing since Sunday.

blocks.text: El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.
Nayib Bukele wrote in a post on X that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.
They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.
They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.
According to Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.
He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".
Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.

A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives.
So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said.
On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack.
It added that it had "engaged armed gang elements, with helicopter support" and that early reports had indicated that several gang members were killed.

Earlier this week, the UN warned that Haiti's armed gangs were adapting to intensified security conditions, saying that they were "stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas".
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and two weeks ago postponed presidential and legislative elections - scheduled for 13 December - indefinitely.
The country has been wracked by economic chaos, a political vacuum and increasingly violent gang warfare since its president was assassinated in 2021.
More than 5,500 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti in 2024. Armed gangs currently control about 85% of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

articles.title: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine
articles.summary: Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace

blocks.text: Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.

Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a monastery.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Thursday that numerous sites across the city had been hit and damaged. Twelve regions across the country were bombed including the southern city of Odesa, where the port was badly hit.

Zelenskyy said the latest devastating strikes showed that Russia was not serious about peace. “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” he said.

blocks.caption: Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people, and wounding 22, including four children. Photograph: Vladislav Musienko/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: During negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Vladimir Putin, who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.

In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply. “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles,” he wrote.

Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors which could bring down enemy missiles and more sanctions against Moscow.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, ⁠Andrii Sybiha, ⁠added that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russian aggression.

On Wednesday, the Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s real intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, leaving millions in the dark and cold, officials in Kyiv believe.

According to Zelenskyy, the US has resumed intelligence warnings of Russian missile attacks. But the White House has so far not reversed the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, leaving Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes.

The New York Times reported that when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.

The decision to cripple Ukraine’s successful drone programme came amid the most serious row between Washington and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. It began after Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, to lower US fuel prices, a move which Zelenskyy branded “weak”.

The Trump administration denies it is deliberately helping the Russians. But European diplomats concede that the US appears to have switched sides. Ukrainian civilians are dying as a result, they say.

Russia, meanwhile, said it had shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones launched in overnight attacks. One man ⁠was ⁠killed ​and another was ⁠wounded as a ⁠result ​of ‌a Ukrainian aerial strike in Russia’s Belgorod region, local ‌authorities said.

Details also emerged of a Ukrainian counterattack through a tunnel in the north-eastern city of Kupiansk, which Russia partly occupies. As part of Operation Veles, the Khartia corps carried out the world’s first underground counteroffensive, advancing 15km into enemy rear lines.

“We observed how the enemy operates underground and studied their methods. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves,” Khartia’s commander, Brig Gen Ihor Obolienskyi , told Ukrainian media.

The Ukrainian soldiers crawled 15km through tunnels – without communication, GPS or light – having developed their own navigation and life-support technologies in advance. About 100 Russians were killed in the operation, and 30 taken prisoner, the Khartia corps said.

articles.title: DOJ says there's possible resurgence of scam hubs
articles.summary: Justice Undersecretary Nicky Ty on Thursday said there may be a resurgence of small-scale scam hub operations in the Philippines following the arrest and rescue of several individuals in various…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 6:12pm

Justice Undersecretary Nicky Ty on Thursday said there may be a resurgence of small-scale scam hub operations in the Philippines following the arrest and rescue of several individuals in various raids.
In early October, authorities rescued more than 230 scam hub workers in Zamboanga Sibugay.

“It’s possible that there is a resurgence, but nevertheless, compared to before mas maliit talaga, not just in the scale of operations but also on the composition of the foreign nationals who are rescued or found within these scam hubs,” Ty, the Undersecretary-in-Charge of IACAT, said at a press briefing.
Ty added that most of the individuals rescued before were mostly Chinese, along with some Vietnamese, Indonesian, Myanmar, Nepalese, and African.
“Ngayon, it’s really mostly Chinese ‘yung mga nahanap natin,” he said.
(Now, we’re finding that it’s really mostly Chinese.)
When asked what could be the reason for this, Ty cited the visa-free arrangement for Chinese nationals, among other reasons.

“Another reason, although nakita ito, na identify ito from the ground, na some Chinese individuals who were located in the scam hubs actually entered the Philippines using the visa-free arrangement. And some of them are actually overstaying,” he said.

(Another reason, although this was seen and identified on the ground, is that some Chinese individuals who were located in the scam hubs actually entered the Philippines using the visa-free arrangement. And some of them are actually overstaying.)
Ty said the Department of Justice (DOJ) is still collecting information.
“Hindi natin maitatanggi, ano, na ‘yang isang privilege na binigay natin sa mga Chinese tourists napagsamantalahan sa problema na ito,” he added.
(We cannot deny that this privilege we granted to Chinese tourists has been exploited in this problem.)
He said the IACAT and DOJ has yet to give its recommendation regarding the visa-free arrangement.
The Philippines retained its Tier 1 ranking in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report. — RSJ, GMA News
