articles.title: EU's Sakharov Prize won by the International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The EU has announced the International Criminal Court as the winner of this year's Sakharov Prize.

image.caption: The ICC was founded in 2002 in The HagueImage: Jiji Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has won this year's Sakharov Prize, awarded by the European Union to individuals and organizations in recognition of their work to support and protect human rights and democracy.
The decision to award the Netherlands-based court, and its officials, was announced by European Parliament President Roberta Metsola.

"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the Court in upholding international law and justice," Metsola said in the European Parliament.
In naming the ICC as the prize winner, Metsola also took time to recognize the two other finalists: Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and the Iranian twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi.
The prize ceremony will take place in December.
What is the International Criminal Court?
Set up in 2002 in the Hague, the ICC is responsible for prosecuting the most serious of crimes, including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The ICC has recently come under sanctions from the US government under President Donald Trump in response to what Washington called political bias. The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The US said it wants to "dismantle" the court.
The awarding of the Sakharov Prize is a further show of support after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
More to come...

articles.title: Police investigate Married at First Sight Australia after 'inappropriate' allegations
articles.summary: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".

blocks.text: A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared.
"Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."
BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.
A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."
Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.

In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.

One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.
Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".
As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.
The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.
In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.
The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.
The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show.
The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.
Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.
Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".
BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.
Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

articles.title: Is PH farmland healthy amid El Niño? FAO calls for soil assessment
articles.summary: With less frequent but more intense tropical cyclones expected in the coming months amid the El Niño phenomenon, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has called for soil assessment in the…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 5:45pm

With less frequent but more intense tropical cyclones expected in the coming months amid the El Niño phenomenon, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has called for soil assessment in the country's farmlands to ensure food security.
Dulce Carandang, FAO Philippines assistant representative for programme, said drought has other aspects other than low rainfall.
"Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater," Carandang said during a press briefing in Makati City on Thursday.
"There may not be rain, but if our groundwater is really secure and it's available, then farmers would be able to produce food," she added.
Based on PAGASA's climate outlook for November 2026 to April 2027, there are 12 areas in the country predicted to experience drought in November.

The state weather bureau said drought occurs when there are three consecutive months of way below (>60% reduction from average) or five consecutive months of below normal (21%-60% reduction from average) rainfall condition.

blocks.caption: 'Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater,' says Dulce Carandang, assistant representative for programme, Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) Philippines, during a press conference in Makati City on Thursday, Octo…

blocks.text: 'Drought isn't just about the lack of rain. We also need to look at the state of our soil, the health of our groundwater,' says Dulce Carandang, assistant representative for programme, Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) Philippines, during a press conference in Makati City on Thursday, October 22, 2026. MARIEL CELINE SERQUIÑA
Part of assessing the soil's health is its ability to absorb nutrients for plants, which could impact the food production.

"What we need to know with agricultural drought, which of course impacts on food production, 'yung, ano ba 'yun? Kamusta na 'yung soil health? Can it still absorb plants?" Carandang told GMA News Online in an interview.
According to the United States Department of Agriculture, soil health is the continued ability of soil to function as a living ecosystem that sustained plants, animals, and humans.
"It plays a critical role in regulating water, filtering pollutants, cycling nutrients, sustaining soil habitats, and promoting plant growth," the US agency said.
Carandang said the Bureau of Soils and Water Management is currently working with concerned agencies in gathering information about the country's state of vegetation.

"Climate science is evolving, it's progressing. And what is critical is that they (farmers) get all this updated information so that they know when to make the adjustment," the FAO official said during the press briefing.

The Department of Agriculture and the Philippine Space Agency recently signed a five-year agreement to use satellite technology to help monitor and protect farms and fishing areas from the effects of El Niño.
The satellite will monitor crop health, map flooding and dry spells, assess irrigation infrastructure, forecast harvests and identify areas at risk of agricultural damage. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
articles.summary: Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.

blocks.text: Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.
Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.

He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.

Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.

Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.
More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.
So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.

On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.
In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.

Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.

For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.

articles.title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
articles.summary: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement which have targeted airports and other sites in the kingdom.

blocks.text: Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.
Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.
The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.
On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces.
Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.
The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.
The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced.

The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

articles.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
articles.summary: Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Which new sectors could revive growth and contain the far-right AfD, whose support has grown…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government set out a high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors, including artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and climate-neutral mobilityImage: NEURA Robotics/pexels.com/@eren-li

blocks.text: Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.
While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.
The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.
Merz seeks growth via advanced tech

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.
These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."
Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.
Germany under pressure
Trillions in new investments

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.
Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.
The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.
He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.
Investors circle future growth sectors

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.
Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.
US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

blocks.caption: China has built more than 2,000 economic zones and industrial parksImage: Liu Quanle/VCG/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A case for special economic zones

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.
"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.
In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.
"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.
Defense spending powers tech growth
The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.
The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
The cost gap need not be decisive

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But it doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.
"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.
"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.

articles.title: Some New Yorkers hail ban on horse-drawn carriages, but drivers fear for incomes
articles.summary: As councillors prepare to banish the vehicles, views in Central Park are divided over the 160-year-old tradition.

blocks.text: After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.

She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horse, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried.

"What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, who has been driving in the park for six years. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"

Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.

On Thursday, New York City Council is expected to vote to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.
But several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban.

"There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."
Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions.
New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers.
But the ban movement found new momentum this summer after the death of a teenager.

In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park.
Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk.

Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years' time.

The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision.
Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation.
"They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals."
Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke.
"I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way."

Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked.
The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment.

The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business.

A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing.
But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the plan did not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out".
The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year.
The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work.
Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being have been raised in the city for decades.

The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse.
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages.

Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand and wait with drivers to be hired. Customers pay $72.22 for a 20-minute ride, plus $28.89 for every extra ten minutes.
Vanessa Stolle, a German tourist, said she and her family had horses at home - and that they do not belong in a noisy park pulling passengers.
"To stand the whole day here – it's loud for them and they can't go to the countryside," she said.

A fellow German tourist, Christian Bauers, disagreed. He remembered seeing the horses when he came to Central Park 20 years ago. "It's part of the culture of New York," he said. "Let them stay. It's cute."
Jeanne Collopy is an animal lover from Colorado, where horses run wild, she said. She worries about accidents in the park that have harmed humans and horses.
"I know there's a union and I hate to have people out of work," she said, adding: "It's a little bit confining for the horses."
Her husband, Chris Koenigs, said the animals were "wonderful" to look at. But the death of the teenager this summer was "sickening", and a high price to pay for enjoying the horses, he said.
"The park is magnificent," he added. "I can't help but think, it would be a magnificent park with or without the carriages."

articles.title: DBM: No funds released under 'unconstitutional' provisions of 2026 budget
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said Thursday it has not yet released any funds charged against the special provisions authorizing unprogrammed appropriations under the 2026 General…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 5:03pm

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said Thursday it has not yet released any funds charged against the special provisions authorizing unprogrammed appropriations under the 2026 General Appropriations Act, which the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional.
Budget Secretary Kim Robert De Leon confirmed this during the Senate Finance subcommittee’s deliberations on the proposed P3.1 billion budget of the DBM for fiscal year 2027.

“On the invalidity of Section 1(a) and 1(b)...the DBM has not released anything charged from 1(a) and 1(b) from the 2026 naman po as of now. So far, wala po tayong charged (we haven’t charged anything) against 1(a) and 1(b) for 2026,” De Leon said.
“Tanging FAPs (foreign-assisted projects) pa lang po ang releases natin from 2026 [unprogrammed appropriations],” he added.
(So far, only the funding for foreign-assisted projects has been released from the 2026 unprogrammed appropriations.)

In a landmark decision, the Supreme Court struck down the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 after Congress added appropriations beyond what the President had recommended in the National Expenditure Program.

Specifically, the 2024 budget was voided due to a P449.5-billion increase in unprogrammed appropriations, while the 2025 budget was struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
The High Court likewise deemed unconstitutional Special Provisions 1(a) and (b) of Chapter XLIII in the 2026 GAA, which authorized unprogrammed appropriations.
It then set conditions that would allow such appropriations to be constitutional.
DBM asked to pause

In a Palace briefing on Thursday, Solicitor General Darlene Berberabe likewise advised the DBM to hold off on implementing the provisions of the 2026 GAA that were deemed unconstitutional by the Supreme Court.
This comes amid the clarification and partial reconsideration that the Office of the Solicitor General would seek on certain parts of the decision.
“Sa amin po, ang ipapayo po namin sa DBM at sa Ehekutibo ay pumorma na tayo na parang huwag muna tutal aasahan natin na madesisyunan ito kaagad,” Berberabe said.
(For our part, we would advise the DBM and the Executive branch to hold off for now, especially since we expect a decision on this matter soon.)
“Siguradong bibigyan din ito ng prayoridad ng ating Supreme Court sapagkat ayaw din naman ng Supreme Court dapat na maapektuhan ‘yung execution ng budget sa ating remaining 2026,” she added.
(The Supreme Court will surely prioritize this as well, as they would not want the execution of the budget for the remainder of 2026 to be affected.)
Safeguards

Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Finance, also sought clarification from the DBM on the implications of the SC decisions for the proposed 2027 budget and the adjustments needed to prevent problems down the line.

“Bagama't hindi idineklara ng Supreme Court na unconstitutional ang unprogrammed appropriations per se, malinaw ang naging paalala nito sa Kongreso: We have a constitutional duty to exercise fiscal discipline, uphold transparency and accountability, and ensure that every appropriation complies with the mandates of our Constitution,” Ejercito said.
(Although the Supreme Court did not declare unprogrammed appropriations as unconstitutional, it issued a clear reminder to Congress.)

“Malinaw po sa inyong lingkod at sa committee na ito ang ating tungkulin (our duty is clear to me and to this committee). We must ensure that the 2027 national budget is not only fiscally sound and responsive to the needs of our people, but also fully compliant with the Constitution,” he continued.
De Leon said the DBM has initial reviews on the matter and would share these with the committee.

“There are also previous references or previous iterations of the special provisions that we can revisit and check kung ito ay papasok po doon sa interpretation na ibinigay ng (to see if they align with the interpretation provided by the) Supreme Court on Section 1(a) and 1(b),” the DBM chief said.
The Senate Finance subcommittee has endorsed for plenary consideration the proposed 2027 budget of the DBM and its attached agencies.
This covers the agency’s lump-sum funds, budgetary support to government-owned and controlled corporations, and allocations to local government units. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Laos-PH drug smuggling mastermind tied to int'l syndicate -- PDEA
articles.summary: The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) on Thursday said the alleged mastermind of the Laos drug smuggling attempt has ties to an international criminal syndicate.

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 4:47pm
The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) on Thursday said the alleged mastermind of the Laos drug smuggling attempt has ties to an international criminal syndicate.
During the House Committee on Dangerous Drugs hearing, PDEA chief Isagani Nerez named former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edrieza Rimbang as the mastermind of the entire attempt.

“Rimbang appears not to be a mere financier, but the person who conceptualized, who planned for the delivery of those illegal drugs from Laos to the Philippines, so he was the one who made those plans, made those suggestions to his conduits, his cohorts, and yes, he provided the needed financial requirement for the chartering of that flight,” Nerez said.

“We suspect that Rimbang has other cohorts. We suspect, and we believe, honestly believe that Rimbang is connected with an international syndicate because the items are coming from another country,” the PDEA chief added.

Nerez said only an international drug syndicate could have accessed the illegal drugs produced in the Golden Triangle, a region where the borders of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet. The area is notorious for drug production and other organized criminal activities.
GMA News Online is trying to reach Rimbang for a statement and will update the story once he responds.
In a DZBB report from Allan Gatus, Police Master Sergeant Aileen Jane Manalo Mendoza, one of the persons of interest in the case, is also suspected of playing a major role in the operation.
Mendoza was the one who allegedly made the arrangements for the plane that would have been used in the drug smuggling.
Meanwhile, the full name of the “Fahad” who was arrested by Lao authorities is Fahad Dibaroson, who is married to the wife of Rimbang’s sister.
Before being arrested in Laos, Dibaroson had traveled to Singapore and Malaysia, according to the PDEA.
On October 1, Lao authorities thwarted P3.5 billion in illegal drugs on a private plane headed to the Philippines.
Thai-PH smuggling?
Aside from the Laos drug smuggling attempt, there were also reports of another shipment of drugs headed towards the Philippines. This time, it was reportedly thwarted in Thailand.
According to Gatus’ report, Nerez also said that there was no evidence showing that the ship was headed to the Philippines.
PDEA said that should it have landed in the Philippines, the agency would have been able to stop it. —RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker?
articles.summary: The most prestigious individual prize in football will be awarded on Monday, with Bayern Munich's English striker Harry Kane the front runner. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite…

image.caption: Harry Kane is already Bayern Munich's seventh top Bundesliga scorerImage: Carina Johansen/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. But for those with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, he was one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or, in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Stammer, in 1996.
That long drought looks set to end on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, the favorite to pick up the trophy at a ceremony held, as a one off, in his native London.

"It's obviously special for me that the ceremony is taking place in London. "I come from London and lived there for a long time — maybe that's a good omen," Kane told club magazine Säbener51. "The Ballon d'Or would be a massive success for me."

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16 looks to be the main competitor. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title.
Kane career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season make for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 158 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," said Vincent Kompany of his striker last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now – it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

At 33, Kane continues to improve at a point where many footballers start to regress. While he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way, and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions Leagueagainst Arsenal on Wednesday. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance, and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all round game. "The pass was one of my best ones. I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals," Kane said postmatch.
Leading from the front

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after he joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023 that: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care, he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone and that is his mindset and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills. He is a complete package," he said last month as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic.

There are detractors who point to perceived 'stat-padding', scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams, and a lot less money, than in England. While Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

blocks.caption: Harry Kane has missed out on international honors with EnglandImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Should Kane win the award, it will be a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga. Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain would make Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward though. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.
Domestic trophies won but international success eludes
For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023 before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential. He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean… With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggest he could get better still.

articles.title: Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign
articles.summary: Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's lack of support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the…

image.caption: Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) are the two frontrunners in the race for the presidency in BulgariaImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Six months after Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the country is gearing up to choose its next president.

Although the role of president in Bulgaria is largely ceremonial, the election on October 25 — with a potential runoff on November 1 — will serve as a test for the government of former President Rumen Radev, whose party won a landslide victory in April, securing an unprecedented majority — the first in Bulgaria in almost three decades.

Although there are 27 candidates on the ballot, the race has narrowed to a duel between the incumbent president, Iliana Yotova, who served two terms as Radev's vice president and is backed by the prime minister, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is supported by opposition parties.
The role of the president

According to the Bulgarian Constitution, the Bulgarian president embodies national unity. He or she represents the country at international level (with a few exceptions), is the commander-in-chief of its armed forces, appoints members of the Supreme Judicial Council and various regulatory bodies, including caretaker governments, and has the power to veto legislation.

blocks.caption: Sunday's presidential election will serve as a test for the government of Rumen Radev. Pictured here: newspaper headlines on the morning after Radev's landslide victory in AprilImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hristo Panchugov, political scientist at the New Bulgarian University in Sofia, argues that although the president's powers are formally limited, the office is particularly significant in the current context.

"For the first time in Bulgaria's modern democratic history, we have an absolutely uncontested majority that is not held together by any coalition, but rather by a single political party that faces an opposition that is completely falling apart," he told DW.
Panchugov went on to say that it would have been better if the campaign had focused more on "whether the president could serve as a counterbalance."

Opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov reiterated this point in an interview with DW: "We are seeing a concentration of power that always bears the marks of a slide toward autocracy," he said, adding that "a president should know how to say no."

blocks.caption: Iliana Yotova, president of Bulgaria (left), has the backing of Prime Minister and former President Rumen Radev (right)Image: BGNES

blocks.text: Iliana Yotova declined DW's request for an interview.
The impact of the war in Ukraine
Initially, the presidential race was characterized by small rallies, a lack of televised debates and numerous personal attacks on the two leading candidates.
In recent weeks, however, following drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea, the two frontrunners' diverging positions on support for Ukraine have come to the fore.
Bulgaria's government initially declined invitations to join the Coalition of the Willing and NATO's anti-drone initiative but changed its position on the latter after the recent drone attacks.
Yotova advocates for the establishment of a "Coalition of Peace," where she says Bulgaria would have a stronger diplomatic voice in ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

"There are many warmongers in our country; I am not one of them," she said at a campaign rally this month, adding that "as long as I am president — and if you place your trust in me — not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine."

Yotova sought to reassure voters that no Bulgarian troops would be sent to Ukraine, even though this was not part of the public debate and despite a 2025 parliamentary declaration that reaffirmed that the Bulgarian Armed Forces would not participate in hostilities there.
Nevertheless, the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea have put new pressure on both the president and Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party.
The effect of the Black Sea drone strikes

"The drone strikes in the Black Sea brought the otherwise abstract geopolitical situation right into the daily lives of every Bulgarian," Boriana Dimitrova, managing partner of the Alpha Research market and social research agency, told DW.

blocks.caption: After a second series of drone attacks on ships in waters off the Bulgarian coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev (center right) summoned the Russian ambassador, Eleonora Mitrofanova (center left), for talksImage: BGNES

blocks.text: Many in Europe, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have laid the blame for the attacks squarely at Russia's door. The fact that Bulgaria's leaders did not clearly attribute blame for the attacks fueled frustration across the country.
After the first drone attack, President Yotova convened the country's Consultative Council on National Security. Its subsequent declaration did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

A week later, after the second attack, Prime Minister Radev said, "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of Russia." He then summoned the Russian ambassador for talks.
Opposition to an 'ambiguous' foreign policy stance
The stance of the government and president is having an impact on the race.

"We're seeing a slight decline in support for Iliana Yotova, which is not threatening her first-place position by any means in the first round, but there has been a decline given the ambiguity of some of the positions she has taken," said Boriana Dimitrova.
As the issue of security entered the public debate, some Bulgarians took to the streets in Sofia to protest against what they saw as the government's ambiguous foreign policy stance on this matter.

"I think the drone attacks in the Black Sea and the utterly spineless stance of the president, the prime minister, and everyone acting in unison were the last straw, and I believe that, on the eve of the presidential election, this should serve as a catalyst," Vlada Tzenova, one of the protesters, told DW.

All this is reflected in the preliminary results of the latest opinion poll conducted by Alpha Research. While expected voter turnout is up, the gap between the two frontrunners has narrowed: Yotova is still ahead, leading Gyurov by about 12 percentage points in the first round, but the margin is smaller than it was.
Who could be the kingmaker?
Nevertheless, these recent dynamics do not necessarily mean a shift in the balance of power.

blocks.caption: Protesters gathered in the Bulgarian capital in late September to voice grievances over the direction of state policies and perceived alignment with RussiaImage: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Political scientist Hristo Panchugov says that Gyurov's campaign has been hampered by his hesitancy to declare his candidacy, a lack of "passion" in his campaign and the fact that he made few comments on current affairs before he joined the race.
Moreover, supporters of the candidate of the pro-Russian nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party, who ranks third in the Alpha Research poll, would be most likely to support Yotova in a second round.

What could decide the outcome of the election is the fact that both GERB and DPS, two of the established parties that attracted the support of more than 660,000 voters in April, did not field a presidential candidate.

According to Alpha Research, half of GERB's supporters do not intend to vote in the first round. The party dominated Bulgaria's political landscape for 17 years but lost power in December following mass anti-corruption protests backed by opposition parties supporting Andrey Gyurov.
Most of the remaining GERB supporters are expected to back Gyurov, as the party has historically opposed Iliana Yotova's political home, the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

At the same time, both Gyurov's campaign and nationalist parties are seeing increased mobilization, with the latter drawing support from voters disappointed by the government's cautious response to the drone attacks.

"We can view these elections as the first test of confidence in the party that recently won the election," Boriana Dimitrova said. "In peaceful times, the center attracts the most attention; in turbulent times, those candidates who take a clearer stance — regardless of the direction — gain greater visibility."

articles.title: Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
articles.summary: Bukangi the shark became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted in a canal in Busan weeks ago.

blocks.text: A famed dusky shark in South Korea is continuing to linger near a canal that it was ejected from on Wednesday.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get her back to the open sea, using nets to guide it out.

On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and instead has been seen circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.
But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.
For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.
Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.
Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.
A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers have concluded their operations to free the shark.

articles.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use, as experts sound the alarm
articles.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far…

image.caption: In a bid to help farmers, the EU has proposed unlimited, open-ended approval for certain pesticidesImage: Andrii Yalanskyi/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.
Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of maximum 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities would bear the responsibility, not the industry.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and to help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.
Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?
The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances." But their stance still proposed extending initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.
The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation." He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.
How do pesticides affect human health, environment?
Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.
Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

blocks.caption: In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to the Agriculture MinistryImage: Adam Berry/Getty Images

blocks.text: When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides." However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: a survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time. "The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge."
More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe nongovernmental organization in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews. That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby. This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group, Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.
Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said. Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.
Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.
Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'?

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products. And that also includes maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides, not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but […] it will not be the silver bullet."

articles.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms
articles.summary: A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.
articles.byline: Dave Seglins, Andreas Wesley, Saloni Bhugra

image.caption: Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages, a new analysis shows. Most of them didn't include information about harm reduction or age restrictions. (David Zalubowski/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."
"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News.
His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated.
One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.
T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.
"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."
Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.
Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

items: Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos

blocks.text: 2-3 ads per minute
A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.
CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages.
Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.

Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.
Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.
Researcher found thousands of gambling messages in NHL games
"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said.

"For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."
He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets.

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute).
Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising.

"Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."
Proposed Canadian ad standards
If Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons.
"It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.

She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.

MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October. (Dave Seglins/CBC)
"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.
Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling.

"These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News.
"We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."
Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed. (Twitter)
Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites.
But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events.
Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling advertisements, restricting them to after 9 p.m.
In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction.
While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations.
Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies.
Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill.
In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future profits.
Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads.

"Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote.
Public health response

A coalition of a dozen mental health organizations, including the Canadian Mental Health Association and Public Health Physicians of Canada, alongside 28 prominent addictions researchers, have sent submissions to Parliament asking for national action.
"The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher and senior research associate at the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction.
"The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."
Addictions researcher Matthew Young is lobbying for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)
"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."

The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has filed its own submission opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.
Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves."

items: CBC Marketplace 2024 study of gambling ads

blocks.text: "Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states.
Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol.
"I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"

articles.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
articles.summary: Disaffection has often driven down turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push to get rid of the right-wing governing coalition.

blocks.text: Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondentReporting fromNazareth

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

blocks.caption: Image caption, All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties

blocks.text: All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties
Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.
A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis

blocks.text: Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.
There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties

blocks.text: Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.
I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word its racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.
These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

blocks.caption: Image caption, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"

blocks.text: United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.
